name: Forms
summary: What a form control is, and how every form control is labelled, described, marked as required and validated, and how a form reports its errors, on every platform.
description: A form control is a component through which people enter or choose a value the product keeps, whether or not it sits in a form that is submitted. Each control is specified on its own page; this foundation says which components are form controls and holds what they share, so that a field behaves the same way next to its neighbours and on every platform: its anatomy (label, description, message), how a required field is marked, which validation statuses exist and how they render, when a value is checked, how errors are announced and summarised, and how fields are spaced. Draft: the rules below describe what the controls do today and what every trusted source agrees on; each open point is decided one step at a time with the team.

specimens.name: Form gaps
specimens.description: The spaces of a form's layout: between two fields, between two groups of fields, between a group's title and its first field, and between a label column and its controls. The actions take the field or the group gap.

rules.name: What a form control is
rules.text: A form control is a component through which people enter or choose a value the product keeps: text, a number, one or several options, on or off, a point in a range. It has a visible label and may have a description; when its value can be missing or wrong, it can be marked required and report an error. Whether the value applies at once or with the rest of the form depends on how the control is used, not on the component.

rules.name: Which rules a control follows
rules.text: Every form control follows the rules on its anatomy and its label. A control that can be marked required also follows the rules on required fields, and a control that can show a severity (it has the severity property, or the error state it sets) also follows the rules on severities, errors and their announcement. Which rules a control follows is read from its specification: its label part, its required property, its severity property and its message part, with no list of exceptions. A control that can be marked required can also show a severity, so a missing or wrong value is said in text next to it: the Search field takes the Text field's severities (forms-search-field-severity). Not decided yet (step 2b): whether the label, required and message guidelines the controls repeat move into this foundation.

rules.name: Form actions
rules.text: A button that submits a form is a form action, not a form control: people activate it, they do not enter or choose a value with it. It does not follow this foundation as a control; the rules about the actions of a form name it in their text.

rules.name: Anatomy of a field
rules.text: A field stacks a visible label, the control, an optional description (format, example, constraint) and, when it shows a severity, a message saying what is wrong and how to fix it, what to check or what was confirmed. The message sits under the description, for every severity: the help and the message are both visible, and the control's aria-describedby lists the description, then the message. A group of checkboxes or radios takes the same parts around its options, with a legend as its label and the message after the options. The message is never in place of the description, the description is not moved above the control, and no line is reserved for the message (that may come back as a choice of the form's layout in step 10). Every form control that can show a severity has a message part, after its description: the Checkbox, which has the error severity but no message part yet, gets it with the complex controls (step 2b); until then it is a known gap the validator warns about.

rules.name: Label
rules.text: Every control has a visible label that stays visible while people type, associated with the control so assistive technology announces it as the control's name. A placeholder is never the label.

rules.name: Where the label sits
rules.text: The anatomy fixes the order (label, control, description, message) and the association; where the label sits is a layout choice. The generic rule, applied as is on the web: the label sits above a field-like control (Text field, Number field, Search field, Textarea, Select) by default; a form may put the labels of its fields in a column at the start. Where the labels sit is a setting of the form, never of a field: labelPlacement, above (the default) or start, set once per form and passed to every field-like control of the form, as markedFields is, so a form never mixes placements, and the form sizes one column for all its labels. A group's legend sits in that column; a checkbox, a radio or a switch keeps its label after the box whatever the setting. A design tool draws the setting outside the component's variants, as markedFields. In the column, every label and every group legend aligns to its end, against its control: the column is as wide as the longest label, at most 14 em (a longer label wraps), and each label ends form.gap.label-column (space.12, 12 px) from its control whatever the other labels' lengths, immediately before its field. A label's first line is centred on the control's box; the description and the message stay under the control; in a right-to-left language start and end mirror, so the labels sit to the right of their fields. By default the column stacks, every label back above its field, when the form itself is narrower than 30 rem (480 px), wherever the form sits (a page, a dialog, a side panel), so it also stacks when people zoom in; a product may keep the column at smaller widths, or move the threshold, when its labels and controls still fit, still without scrolling in two dimensions at a width of 320 CSS px. On iOS and Android the column also stacks at the largest text sizes; a checkbox, a radio or a switch has its label after the box; the label never sits inside the box, so there is no floating label on the web. On iOS, Android and desktop, a control follows its platform's own requirements and constraints where the platform has them, and the generic rule where it has none: a floating label is allowed where it is that platform's standard way, such as Material's text field label on Android; on Windows, whose Forms guidance places labels above the input control, the labels stay above whatever the form's setting.

rules.name: Required fields
rules.text: A required field is exposed as required to assistive technology (the required attribute on the web) and marked visibly before people submit, never by color alone. The generic rule, applied as is on the web, marks the fewer fields: by default, when a form has more required fields than optional ones (or as many), required fields carry no mark, each optional field ends its label (or its group's legend) with "(optional)", and a note before the first field says "All fields are required unless marked optional."; when a form has more optional fields than required ones, each required field ends its label (or legend) with "(required)" instead, and no note is needed. No asterisk. Which fields a form marks is a rule of the form: every control that can be marked required carries the same property, markedFields (optional, required, none; optional by default), set once per form to the same value, and draws its mark from its own required: "(optional)" when it is not required and the form marks optional fields, "(required)" when it is required and the form marks required fields, nothing with none (a control outside a form, such as a filter; the default of the Search field, which usually stands alone). The note before the first field is the form's. The mark follows the label (or the legend) after a word space, at its size, in the regular weight and the description's color, the disabled text color when the control is disabled. On Android and Windows the asterisk is red, the color of the error message and icon, at the label's size and weight, 4 px after the label (2 px in small), and so is the asterisk of the note that explains it. On the web, "(required)" is hidden from assistive technology, since the required attribute already exposes the state, so it is said once; "(optional)" stays in the label's text, so it is part of the accessible name, since no attribute says that a field is optional. Each platform applies its own guidance where it has some, and the generic rule where it has none: on Android, as Material asks, each required field ends its label (or legend) with an asterisk, explained once before the first field and included in the accessibility label; on Windows, as its Forms guidance asks, each required field ends its label with an asterisk, explained once before the first field, and sets AutomationProperties.IsRequiredForForm; iOS and macOS, where Apple gives no mark, apply the generic rule. Wherever the platform exposes a required state (the required attribute on the web, IsRequiredForForm on Windows, accessibilityRequired on macOS), the state says the field is required and a visible "(required)" is hidden from assistive technology; on Windows the asterisk stays in the accessible name, since Microsoft asks that the name be the label as shown; on iOS, where no accessibility trait says required, "(required)" stays in the accessibility label. A required Checkbox group means at least one option checked: no box carries the required state, since on a checkbox it requires that very box (on one box, that option; on every box, all of them); the product checks the group when the form is submitted and its error says so ("Choose at least one"). Its legend's "(required)" is not hidden from assistive technology on the web, since no state says that a group is required (aria-required is not supported on the group role of a fieldset), so it is part of the group's name. A set of consents that must all be accepted is a set of separate required Checkboxes, not a required group. A Radio group keeps the platform's required state: a required radio makes its whole group required, and its legend's "(required)" stays hidden on the web.

rules.name: Severities
rules.text: A form control can show one of three severities, none by default: an error says the value is not accepted and how to fix it, a warning says the value is accepted but deserves attention, a success says the value was checked and confirmed, by a check people cannot make themselves (rule timing). The word is "error", not "invalid": every platform's guidance speaks of errors (WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification, the Compose error semantics, Material's error text), while invalid is the web's technical term. There is no information severity: information that holds before any check is the description's job, and no source gives a field an information status. The property is severity, and one message carries every severity. The Checkbox, the Checkbox group and the Radio group have only the error severity: a choice has nothing to confirm or to warn about (our judgment, not a source's). On the web, the error is aria-invalid="true" (and :user-invalid when the browser validates); a warning and a success have no web state, since aria-invalid has no value for them: they are the message text and the styling. The control's border takes the severity's accent functional border color and the message its functional text color. Since the Color foundation 7.1.0 (decision border-accent-functional-3-to-1) the accent borders reach the 3:1 of WCAG 1.4.11 on every surface level; on the subtle warning fill the light warning border was 2.95:1 until the Color foundation set it to the warning text's step, warning 600 (decision border-accent-warning-600): 5.86:1.

rules.name: Severity in the fill
rules.text: The severity is also shown in the control's fill, a solid color, never translucent: the subtle functional background of the severity, global.bg.subtle.functional.<severity>.default (error, warning, success), at rest and on hover alike (step 6, the Text field family as the reference rendering). A hover tint does not apply in a severity: the error hover step (global.bg.subtle.functional.error.hover) would bring the placeholder under 4.5:1 in light mode (4.33:1, WCAG 1.4.3), and every severity behaves the same. The value and the placeholder keep their colors on the fill. Every border passes against its fill: error 5.45:1 (light) and 5.14:1 (dark), warning 5.86:1 and 8.27:1, success 7.17:1 and 6.16:1. The choice controls (Checkbox, Checkbox group, Radio group) follow it in their empty boxes: an unchecked box in error takes the subtle error fill inside its error border, at rest and on hover; a checked or indeterminate box keeps its brand fill, so checked still reads checked (forms-choice-error-fill).

rules.name: Severity icon
rules.text: The severity icon is optional and appears in one place only, never inside the area where people type, because browsers add their own elements there (autofill, password manager, reveal, clear, spin and picker controls). Three placements: after the control, centred on it (on its first line for a multi-line control, the Textarea), which narrows the control; at the start of the message, before its text, the control keeping its full width; or none, and then the message's own words say the severity (message-wording). The component never writes a severity word, since it cannot know where a message comes from; with an icon, the icon's name says the severity, so a message does not start with the word, which would be said twice. The placement is a rule of the form, not of each field: every form control that can show a severity carries the same property, severityIcon (after-control, message, none; message by default), and a form sets it once, to the same value, for all its controls, so its fields never mix two placements. The choice controls (Checkbox, Checkbox group, Radio group and any control whose label sits beside its box) draw no icon after the control, because the label or the options follow it there: they offer message and none, and a form set to after-control shows their icon in the message. The text-entry and picker controls (Text field, Number field, Textarea, Search field, Select) offer all three. Its glyph says the severity, the Alert's intent icons and the Figma prototype's: error for an error, warning for a warning, check_circle for a success, so the three severities differ by shape as well as color; it is named after its severity ("Error", "Warning", "Success"), translated with the form's language. Its size: after the control, the icon of the Button of the same size (20, 24 and 24 px for small, medium and large: size.3, size.4, size.4), space.8 after the control and centred on it (on the first line of a multi-line control), as a field lines up with the Button of its size; in the message, the Icon's small size (16 px, size.2, its size next to 14 and 16 px body text), space.4 before the text and centred on its first line. Its color is the on-base icon role of its severity, global.icon.on-base.functional.<severity>.default, the role of an icon on a surface, where it sits in both placements (never on the fill), and the color of the message text: for the error #C01619 in light mode, #F88275 in dark mode, 5.81:1 and 5.30:1 at the lowest on the surface levels; for the warning #765818 and #FFC61C, 6.16:1 and 8.38:1; for the success #075D33 and #11C772, 7.44:1 and 5.92:1 (WCAG 1.4.11); the Search field takes the property with its severities (forms-search-field-severity), the Checkbox with its message part (step 2b).

rules.name: Width without the icon
rules.text: Without the icon after the control (severityIcon message or none, or a choice control), the control keeps its default width and takes the whole width; the place after the control is not reserved. With after-control, the control gives up the icon and the gap after it.

rules.name: A severity is said in text
rules.text: An error is identified in text next to the control it concerns, associated with that control, and never shown by color alone. The text says what is wrong and, when a fix is known, how to fix it. A warning and a success are said in text the same way, whatever icon or color accompanies them.

rules.name: A message says the fix
rules.text: A message tells people what to do, in plain words, the same way for every control and every severity. An error is the instruction that fixes it: the control's verb (enter, choose, check, include) with the format or the limit that fixes it when there is one ("Include an @, as in name@example.com", "Enter a number between 1 and 99", "Choose one"), rather than a statement of what is wrong. A message sits under its label and relies on it: it does not repeat the field's name, which the label already says, on screen and as the control's accessible name read before the message. An empty required field gets a message like any other error ("Enter it as on your ID", "Choose one"), never "This field is required": the form already said which fields are required. A warning says what to check ("Check the domain: did you mean example.com?") and a success what was confirmed ("This one is available"). A message addresses people as you, without blame, without robotic words such as invalid, without interjections such as oops, without please and without we. Without a severity icon (severityIcon none), these words alone make the severity clear, since nothing but color says it otherwise: the fix of an error, what to check for a warning, what was confirmed for a success. This is a guideline the component cannot enforce: a project that cannot write its own messages (they come from a backend it cannot change, or they do not say their severity) adapts them itself, starting them with the severity's word and its language's colon ("Error: …", "Erreur : …" in French) unless they already start with it; the component writes no word and checks nothing (severity-icon). A message and a description are one sentence in sentence case, a second only when the fix needs it, about one line at the field's default width and two lines at most. A single sentence ends with no period ("Choose a country", "We send the receipt to this address"); with two or more sentences, every sentence ends with its period ("Enter at least 20 characters. You have entered 10."); a question keeps its question mark ("Check the domain: did you mean example.com?"). Assistive technology gets the description and the message as one string joined by a space (aria-describedby), so without a period the two run on when read ("…to this address Enter an email…"); a severity icon's name falls between them, none does with severityIcon none. In an error summary, the entry of a field adds the name the inline message leaves out: the field's label verbatim, without its required or optional mark, a colon, a space, then the message with its own casing ("Country: Choose one", "Email address: Include an @, as in name@example.com"), the whole entry a link to the field; an entry whose message is empty shows the label alone, still as a link, so the summary always says which field is in error even when a backend sends no message or the same bare code for several fields. The message is written once and the summary composes the entry, so the field and the summary never disagree. On Android, a message read on its own, without its field (Material gives the error text an alert role, announced when it appears), loses the name it relies on: the field still reads the error with its label when focused (compose-error-components), and the summary names it.

rules.name: When a value is checked
rules.text: By default, as the recommended experience: a field shows an error when people leave it after changing it, and every field is checked when people submit the form, so a required field people skipped shows its error only then; a field never shows a new error while people are typing in it, and an error clears as people type, as soon as the value is right; a new error then waits until they leave the field again. A choice (a checkbox, a radio, an option in a list) is checked when people make it, since choosing commits the value. A check people try values against, such as an available user name or password rules, may run as they type. Some use cases cannot follow the default (a check only the server can make, a value checked as it is entered by its nature); they choose another timing, and still never mark a control as in error before people used it or before validation ran. A warning follows the error's timing, since its value is checked the same way: it shows when people leave a field they changed, or on submit, and clears as they type; the value being accepted, a warning never blocks the submit. A success shows only for a check people cannot make themselves, such as an available user name or a verified code, when that check runs; a field whose value merely passes its checks shows no success. The submit button stays enabled while required fields are empty, so that people can submit and learn what is missing (the generic rule, applied as is on the web and on Android); on iOS, macOS and Windows, whose guidance asks for it, it is disabled until the required fields are filled, the required marks telling people what keeps it disabled.

rules.name: How errors are announced
rules.text: When an error appears as people leave a field, focus already on the next one, the form announces it politely: the field's label, a colon, a space, then the message ("Email address: Include an @, as in name@example.com"), the same string as the field's error summary entry (message-wording), so the announcement says which field it concerns even though the message relies on its label. Politely, so that it waits for the name of the field people just reached instead of interrupting it; the error is checked again when people submit. The form owns this announcement, as it owns the summary, not the control: on the web, one hidden polite live region per form, present in the initial markup; on iOS and macOS, an accessibility announcement at low priority; on Android, a polite live region; on Windows, an element whose LiveSetting is Polite. The field still exposes its error with it (web-rendering, error semantics), read when people come back to it. A warning shown as people leave a field, and a success from a check people cannot make themselves, shown when that check runs (timing), are announced the same way, politely, through the same region or announcement: the label, a colon, a space, then the message ("Email address: Check the domain: did you mean example.com?", "Username: This one is available"). An error that clears as people type is silent: people hear their own keystrokes, the field no longer reads as in error when they come back to it, and the submit checks every field again. After a failed submit, focus moves: to the title of the form's error summary when the form has one, so people hear how many errors it lists ("There are 2 errors in this form") then every entry, "Label: message", each a link to its field (summary); to the first field in error when it has none, which reads its label and its error. Focus moves once per submit, and the summary or the field taking focus is announced by that move, with no live region. On the web, the summary's title takes focus with focus() and tabindex="-1", or, on a page the server sends back, with the autofocus attribute and no script (summary); on iOS and macOS, a layout-changed notification with the summary as the element to move to, or an accessibility focus state; to a field, its focus state, with the layout-changed notification; on Android, a FocusRequester; on Windows, the element's Focus method with the focus state Programmatic. Each platform follows its own guidance where it has some (when to check a value on Apple, Material's error semantics on Android, the marked fields of Windows), and the behaviour above where it has none, through the API its guideline names; no Apple, Android or Windows page says how a form's errors reach the screen reader or where focus goes after a failed submit, so those APIs are the system's judgment, and every guideline that rests on one ends by saying so. The system sets the default, the platforms follow their own guidance, and a product can still depart from both at the end for its own specifics: the default is the rule until it does.

rules.name: Error summary
rules.text: An error summary is optional, never mandatory: a list of the form's errors above its fields, each entry a link to its field. By default, a form shows one after a failed submit when two fields or more are in error; with one error it shows none, and focus moves to that field (announcement). A product may decide never to show one, as a short form such as a sign-in with an email and a password does: this is the product override of the default (announcement). No source gives a number of errors from which to list them: the WAI tutorial, G139 and SCR32 list any number, and WCAG 3.3.1 mandates no particular way, so the form meets it with or without a summary. When the form shows one, the rules it already has apply: its title takes focus after a failed submit (announcement), each entry is the field's label, a colon, then its message, as a link to the field (message-wording), and the form announces the rest as it does without one (announcement). After people fix one of two errors and submit again, one error is left: the summary goes and focus moves to that field. No Apple, Android or Windows page says whether a form lists its errors, so the default applies on every platform. A dedicated Error summary component renders it, not the Alert: an alert must not affect keyboard focus (APG Alert pattern), and WAI-ARIA asks for an alertdialog, not an alert, when focus moves to a message, while the summary's title takes focus. So the summary has no alert role, its title takes focus, and its entries are links. Its title states how many errors the form has: "There are 3 errors in this form", the WAI tutorial's example heading, one sentence with no period (message-wording). The number is the number of entries, one per field in error. The title states and the entries say the fix: the title is not a message, so the rule that a message says the fix applies to each entry, never to the title. The Error summary component holds this English title as its default, and the product passes its own, translated and pluralised: one plural string per language, whose form the language's plural rules pick from the number (English has two forms, one and other; Arabic has six), never a number joined to a word. By default a summary lists two errors or more, yet the string carries every form of its language, for a product that shows one with a single error. It lists the errors only: one entry per field in error, in the order the fields appear in the form. A warning never blocks the submit (timing), so it stays under its field and the summary leaves it out; the title counts exactly the entries. On the web, each entry is a plain in-page link to its field, with no script: <a href="#id">, the id being the field's control. For a group, the link names the group's first option, never its fieldset, which cannot take focus. Following the link, the browser scrolls the control to the top of the view and focuses it (HTML, scrolling to a fragment). To keep the label in view, each field's control carries a top scroll margin (CSS scroll-margin-top) at least as tall as its label, or its group's legend, and the gap above the control: the browser then stops that much higher, and the label shows above the focused field. The system uses the platform's native means first: no script on the web where the browser gives the same result. Two trade-offs come with it: each activation adds a fragment to the URL and an entry to the history, so Back walks through the fields before leaving the page; and a single-page app whose router takes over # links may need its own handling, the product's choice. iOS, Android and desktop have no in-page link: activating an entry moves focus to the field with the means the rule announcement names (a layout-changed notification with the field, a FocusRequester, the Focus method with the focus state Programmatic), the field and its label scrolled into view; no Apple, Android or Windows page says so, so this is the system's judgment. The scroll margin is built with the Error summary component, on the field controls, in #129; this foundation states the behaviour. The component is built in its own pull request after this foundation (#129). It sits at the top of the form, inside it: the first thing after the form's heading and introduction, above the first field, so the summary comes before the fields it lists and the visual, reading and focus orders agree; after its last entry, Tab reaches the first field. A form in a dialog or a panel shows it at the top of that form, never at the top of the page behind it. On a page that is only the form, this is the top of the page before the form, where the WAI tutorial and G139 put it; SCR32 puts it at the top of the form. Its title is a heading one level below the form's heading, or below the page's when the form has none. On iOS, Android and desktop, it is the first element of the form's scrolling content, above the first field, and scrolls with it, never pinned; no Apple, Android or Windows page says where, so this is the system's judgment. Its place needs no script on the web. It shows the errors of the last submit. Fixing a field clears that field's error as the rule timing says, but does not change the summary: its title and its entries stay those of the last submit until people submit again. Each submit checks every field and rebuilds it, its count and its entries, and its title takes focus; when one error is left, the summary goes and focus moves to that field; when none is left, the form is sent. This default holds whoever checks the values, the browser, the app or the server, and needs no script beyond the submit's own. A product whose every check runs in the browser or in the app may update it live instead: an entry leaves the summary when its field is fixed, the title's count follows and the new title is announced politely, through the form's live region or announcement (announcement), and the summary goes when no entry is left. This costs script on every field. Never when a check waits for the server: only a new submit tells whether such a field is fixed, so a live summary would be half up to date. Each platform follows its own guidance on when a value is checked. On iOS and macOS, Apple asks to verify values as soon as people enter them and to give feedback as soon as a problem is detected, so a form whose every check runs in the app may follow that guidance with the live summary, its count announced at low priority. On Android, Android Developers validates a field as people type, so the same holds there, the count in a polite live region. Windows asks to mark the invalid controls on submission and to require a resubmit: the default; a Windows form that applies each value at once, such as a settings page, has no submit and no summary. On iOS, macOS and Windows the submit button stays disabled until the required fields are filled (timing), so a summary there lists values to fix, never empty required fields. No Apple, Android or Windows page speaks of a list of errors: each platform's use is the system's judgment, drawn from when that platform checks a value. The system sets the default, the platforms follow their own guidance, and a product can still override both for its own specifics. On the web, a page the server sends back with errors focuses the summary's title, or the only field in error, with the HTML autofocus attribute, with no script: the attribute applies to every element, so the title keeps its tabindex="-1" and carries autofocus, and one element per page carries it. Its limit: the browser skips autofocus when the page's URL holds a fragment naming an element, so the URL of that page, the form's action or a redirect, carries no fragment; a browser may also skip it once people have started typing. iOS, Android and desktop get the server's answer on the same screen, with no page sent back: once it arrives with errors, focus moves with the means the rule announcement names. A page the server sends back with errors also starts its title with the count: "3 errors – " then the page's own title ("3 errors – Delivery details – Checkout"; with one error, "1 error – Delivery details – Checkout"), so a screen reader says it as soon as the page loads, and the tab and the history show it. The product holds this count as one plural string per language, like the summary's title. After a check the browser or the app runs, or a live update of the summary, no page is loaded: the page's title stays as it is, and the focused summary gives the count. iOS, Android and desktop never load a new screen for a submit: a screen or a window keeps its title, which names where people are (a window's title on iOS and macOS, a pane title on Android, the title bar on Windows), and the focused summary gives the count; no Apple, Android or Windows page speaks of errors in a title, so this is the system's judgment.

rules.name: Spacing
rules.text: Two fields of a form stack form.gap.field (space.16, 16 px) apart, at every field size, from the bottom of a field's last part (its control, description or message) to the next field's label. A field here is any form control with its label, a Checkbox group or a Radio group included: a group of options is one control. The label then sits closer to its own control than to the field above it. Two groups of fields, sections of a form with their own title (such as a delivery address), stack form.gap.group (space.32, 32 px) apart, twice the field gap, from the bottom of a group's last field to the next group's title, and a group's title sits form.gap.title (space.12, 12 px) above its first field, closer to its fields than they are to each other, so it reads as theirs. A Checkbox group or a Radio group is not a group of fields: it takes the field gap. The space shows the grouping, and the structure carries it too (a fieldset and its legend on the web), never the space alone. The form's actions (its submit button and the buttons next to it) take the gap of what precedes them: form.gap.field after a form without groups, form.gap.group after a grouped form, with no token of their own, since they act on the whole form and not on its last group; the buttons stand space.8 (8 px) apart. The values hold on every platform: Windows, whose Forms page spaces input controls 24 px apart and groups of controls 48 px apart, keeps 16 and 32 px, recorded differences and not platform values. These gaps, with the label column's (form.gap.label-column, rule label-placement), are semantic tokens the design system adds (the Figma library has none for them), the same on every platform today; a platform may override them, none does. Inside a field, the label, the control, the description and the message are 6 px apart (space.6, each component's own gap token). A group takes the same 6 px from its legend to its options when there is no description, from its description to its options and from its options to its message; its description sits right under its legend (0 px), the two read as one heading, and its options stack 4 px apart (16 px in a row), closer than the parts around them, so the list reads as one unit. These are component values, the same on every platform: on iOS each option row is at least 44 pt tall and on Android 48 dp (Material sets it), both keeping 4 between rows; macOS keeps the web's values, its 20 pt minimum met; Windows' Spacing page gives 8 epx between a control and its header and 12 epx between a control and its label, a recorded difference a product may override.

rules.name: Keyboard in a form
rules.text: People move through a form's fields from the keyboard in their reading order, on every platform. A form that is submitted has a submit button, and Enter (Return) in a single-line field submits it; a multi-line field takes Enter as a new line. Where the submit button is disabled until the required fields are filled (iOS, macOS and Windows, rule timing), Enter (Return) does not submit the form while it is disabled. A search field that stands alone, the only field of its search form, needs no submit button: Enter runs the search, and the Search field labels its own return key for search. The label of the on-screen keyboard's return key is the form's, set on each single-line field through the platform's own setting for its place in the form: on the web, where Enter submits from every single-line field and enterkeyhint changes only the label, it names the form's action (go, send, search, done) and never next; on iOS and Android, next on every field but the last, whose return key names the form's action and submits the form (Android's Next moves focus by itself, iOS moves it in the field's submit action). Desktop keyboards have no on-screen return key.

rules.name: Web rendering
rules.text: A label element pointing at the control's id; the description and the message referenced by aria-describedby for every severity; the required attribute on a required control; aria-invalid="true" on a control in error and only then; data-severity on the component for the three severities; a fieldset and its legend around a group of checkboxes or radios.

contrast.description: The message of an error on every surface level. Measured only while the severities are being rendered (WCAG 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1). It is also the required asterisk on Android and Windows (decision forms-asterisk-style): 6.12 / 5.79 / 6.12 / 5.79:1 in light mode and 7.06 / 6.47 / 5.92 / 5.30:1 in dark mode.

The message of a warning on every surface level (WCAG 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1): 6.49 / 6.16 / 6.49 / 6.16:1 in light mode and 11.17 / 10.23 / 9.36 / 8.38:1 in dark mode, since the Color foundation's decision warning-on-base-600; the color of the warning icon. A requirement since the warning rendering was decided.

The message of a success on every surface level (WCAG 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1): 7.87 / 7.44 / 7.87 / 7.44:1 in light mode and 7.89 / 7.23 / 6.62 / 5.92:1 in dark mode, the color of the success icon. A requirement since the success rendering was decided.

The border that identifies a control in error, the accent functional border, against every surface level (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1): 6.12 / 5.79 / 6.12 / 5.79:1 in light mode and 4.97 / 4.55 / 4.16 / 3.73:1 in dark mode on levels 0 to 3, since the Color foundation 7.1.0. A requirement since the error rendering was decided (forms-error-fill).
The border of a control in error against its own fill, the other color next to it (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1): 5.45:1 in light mode, 5.14:1 in dark mode.
The value typed in a control in error, on its fill (WCAG 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1): 16.91:1 in light mode, 11.67:1 in dark mode.

The placeholder of an empty control in error, on its fill (WCAG 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1): 5.42:1 in light mode, 6.62:1 in dark mode. On the error hover step it would be 4.33:1 in light mode, so the fill does not change on hover.

The border of a control with a warning against its own fill, the other color next to it (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1): 5.86:1 in light mode (warning 600 since the Color foundation's decision border-accent-warning-600; it was 2.95:1), 8.27:1 in dark mode.
The value typed in a control with a warning, on its fill (WCAG 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1): 17.15:1 in light mode, 11.54:1 in dark mode.
The placeholder of an empty control with a warning, on its fill (WCAG 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1): 5.50:1 in light mode, 6.55:1 in dark mode.
The border of a control with a success against its own fill, the other color next to it (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1): 7.17:1 in light mode, 6.16:1 in dark mode.
The value typed in a control with a success, on its fill (WCAG 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1): 17.30:1 in light mode, 11.43:1 in dark mode.
The placeholder of an empty control with a success, on its fill (WCAG 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1): 5.55:1 in light mode, 6.48:1 in dark mode.

The error icon, after the control or in the message, on every surface level (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1 of a graphic that carries meaning): 6.12 / 5.81 / 6.12 / 5.81:1 in light mode and 7.06 / 6.47 / 5.92 / 5.30:1 in dark mode.

The warning icon, after the control or in the message, on every surface level (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1 of a graphic that carries meaning): 6.49 / 6.16 / 6.49 / 6.16:1 in light mode and 11.17 / 10.23 / 9.36 / 8.38:1 in dark mode, the color of the warning message (Color foundation, decision warning-on-base-600).

The success icon, after the control or in the message, on every surface level (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1 of a graphic that carries meaning): 7.87 / 7.44 / 7.87 / 7.44:1 in light mode and 7.89 / 7.23 / 6.62 / 5.92:1 in dark mode.

The border of a control with a warning, the accent functional border, against every surface level (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1): 6.49 / 6.16 / 6.49 / 6.16:1 in light mode and 8.09 / 7.41 / 6.78 / 6.07:1 in dark mode on levels 0 to 3, since the Color foundation's decision border-accent-warning-600. A requirement since the warning rendering was decided.

The border of a control with a success, the accent functional border, against every surface level (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1): 7.87 / 7.44 / 7.87 / 7.44:1 in light mode and 6.08 / 5.57 / 5.10 / 4.57:1 in dark mode. A requirement since the success rendering was decided.

The required mark, "(optional)" or "(required)", in the description's color on every surface level (WCAG 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1): 12.78 / 12.09 / 12.78 / 12.09:1 in light mode and 8.86 / 8.11 / 7.43 / 6.65:1 in dark mode (decision forms-mark-style).

guidelines.text: A control through which people enter or choose a value has a visible label or instructions whether or not it sits in a form that is submitted; a link or a control not associated with data entry does not.
Activating a button that submits a form is not changing the setting of a control: entering text, checking a box or choosing an option in a list is, and does not submit the form by itself.
A button contributes to the submitted data only when it is the one that submitted the form.
A form either applies each value at once (a settings page) or collects the values and applies them when people choose to submit; the same input controls serve both.
On macOS, a switch can sit in a grouped form, where a mini switch controls the setting of a single row.
Every control has a visible label or instructions, associated with it programmatically.
Related controls are grouped, and the group has a name: a set of radios always, a set of checkboxes or related fields when it helps.
A required field is indicated visibly, not only programmatically and never by color alone; a symbol used to mark it is explained before its first use.
When an input error is detected, the field in error is identified and the error is described in text; color or an icon may add to the text, never replace it.
A warning and a success are said in text like an error, never by color or an icon alone, and a confirmation that appears without moving focus is exposed as a status message.
Set aria-invalid="true" for an error only: it has no value for a warning or a success, which the message text says.
When a correction is known, the error message suggests it, unless that would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.
An error message tells people how to fix the error, close to the field and without blame, rather than only saying what is wrong; a warning says what to check and a success what was confirmed.

A message or a description is one sentence, a second only when the fix needs it, about one line at the field's default width and two lines at most. A single sentence ends with no period, two or more sentences each end with their period, and a question keeps its question mark.

A message relies on the label it sits under and does not repeat the field's name. An error summary references the label of each field: its entry is the label, a colon, then the message, as an in-page link to the field; an entry without a message is the label alone, still a link.
A control is marked as in error only after its value was validated, not before people used it.

By default, a field shows an error when people leave it after changing it, and every field is checked on submit; checking a format while people type would show an error most of the time, so a new error waits until they leave the field, while an error clears as soon as the value is right. A check people try values against, such as an available user name, may run as they type.

A control's user validity turns true when people commit a change (they leave the field) or submit the form, and :user-invalid then follows the value as they type, both ways; so a product that styles errors with :user-invalid alone shows one again mid-typing, and keeps a cleared error hidden until people leave the field to follow the default.

Apple validates when it makes sense for the field, an email address when people switch to another field, and gives feedback as soon as it detects a problem so people can correct it right away: the default checks a field when people leave it and clears its error as soon as the value is right.
On Android, a field can be checked as people move on from it, in the action of the keyboard's Next key, which keeps moving focus to the next field.

On Windows, a number box evaluates its value on loss of focus or Enter, a password box is validated as people type or once they finish, and a submitted form marks the controls whose input is invalid; the default applies, a field checked when people leave it and every field on submit.

A warning shows and clears when an error would, when people leave a field they changed or submit the form, since its value is checked the same way; no source gives a warning a timing of its own, and the value being accepted, it never blocks the submit. A success shows only for a check people cannot make themselves, such as an available user name, when that check runs; a field whose value merely passes gets no success, since people only need to know when something is wrong.

Apple confirms that a task has completed only when it is significant enough, since people only need to know when it does not: a field confirms only a check people cannot make themselves, and shows no success when its value merely passes.

The submit button stays enabled while required fields are empty: submitting shows the error of every required field left empty. On the web a disabled button would leave the tab order, a form whose default button is disabled is not submitted with Enter, and an inactive button is exempt from contrast, so people would not find out what is missing.
Apple makes a button such as Next or Continue available only after people enter the data the app requires: on iOS and macOS the submit button is disabled until the required fields are filled.

Windows disables the submit button until all required information is filled in, and marks the controls whose data is invalid on submission: on Windows the submit button is disabled until the required fields are filled.
A message that reports errors or a result without moving focus, such as the number of errors in a form, is exposed as a status message so assistive technology announces it.

An error that appears as people leave a field, focus already on the next one, is a status message: the form announces it without moving focus, as the field's label, a colon and the message, the same string as its error summary entry, so the field in error is identified; politely, since an interruption is only for what is imperative and may cut off the name of the field people reached.

A warning shown as people leave a field and a success from a check people cannot make themselves are status messages too, a warning on the existence of a problem and the result of an action: the form announces them like an error that appears on leaving a field, politely, as the field's label, a colon and the message, without moving focus. An error that clears as people type is not announced: a live region treats removals as irrelevant by default and keeps them for important changes, the field no longer exposes an error when people come back to it, and the submit checks again. No Apple, Android or Windows page covers announcing a warning, a success or a cleared error: every platform uses the means chosen for an error.

A list of the form's errors at its top, each entry a link to its field, is optional: the WAI tutorial finds it helpful when errors occur, G139 and SCR32 list any number of errors, and WCAG 3.3.1 mandates no particular way of showing them, at the start of the form, inline next to each field, in an alert or in a dialog. By default the form lists its errors when two fields or more are in error after a failed submit; with one, focus moves to that field, which reads its label and its message. A product may decide never to list them, in a short form such as a sign-in.

The error summary is not an alert. An alert must not affect keyboard focus, and when focus moves to a message, WAI-ARIA asks for an alertdialog instead of an alert; the summary's title takes focus after a failed submit, so the summary carries no alert role and is announced by the focus move itself. A dedicated Error summary component renders it: a title that takes focus and a list of links to the fields.

The error summary's title states how many errors the form has, "There are 3 errors in this form", as the WAI tutorial's example heading does and as SCR32's heading counts them: a statement in one sentence with no period, while each entry below it says the fix. The product passes the title in its own language as one plural string, never a number joined to a word: languages have from one to six plural forms (English two, one and other; Arabic six), and the language's plural rules pick the form from the number.

Each entry of the error summary is an in-page link to its field's control, as the WAI tutorial and G139 describe. Following a link to a fragment, the browser scrolls the target into view with block "start", then runs the focusing steps with the document's viewport as the fallback: the control takes focus at the top edge of the view, its label above it, out of view, and a link to a fieldset, which is not focusable, focuses nothing. So an entry for a group names its first option, and the control carries a top scroll margin (scroll-margin-top) that keeps its label or legend in view. Navigating to a fragment pushes a history entry, so each entry followed adds one.

The error summary sits at the top of the form, before its first field: the WAI tutorial lists errors at the top of the page, before the form, and G139 describes a text at the top of the page, both on a page that is the form, while SCR32 displays the list at the top of the form. Before the fields it lists, the summary keeps a reading sequence that makes sense and a focus order that preserves meaning: from the title, Tab goes through the entries to the first field.

The error summary reports the last submit: each submit checks every field and rebuilds the list, as SCR32 builds it in the form's submit handler and replaces an existing list with the new one, and as the WAI tutorial gives its feedback when a form is submitted. Between two submits, fixing a field does not change the summary. A product whose every check runs in the browser or the app may update it live instead: an entry leaves when its field is fixed and the title's count follows; a status text that stays on the page and changes is usually a new status message, so the new title is announced politely, without moving focus. Never when a check waits for the server: only a new submit tells whether such a field is fixed.

Apple asks apps to verify values as soon as people enter them and to give feedback as soon as a problem is detected: on iOS and macOS, a form whose every check runs in the app may follow that guidance with the live error summary, its new title posted as a low-priority announcement; a form with a check the server makes keeps the summary of the last submit. The submit button being disabled until the required fields are filled, the summary lists values to fix, never empty required fields. No Apple page speaks of a list of errors: this use is the system's judgment.

Android Developers validates a field as people type, its error state derived from its value, and runs a check when people move to the next field: on Android, a form whose every check runs in the app may follow it with the live error summary, its new title in a polite live region; a form with a check the server makes keeps the summary of the last submit. No Android page speaks of a list of errors: this use is the system's judgment.

Windows asks to mark the controls with invalid input on submission and to require people to resubmit the form: on Windows the error summary shows the errors of the last submit, the default, and with the submit button disabled until the required information is filled in, it lists values to fix, never empty required fields. A form that updates instantly, as a settings page, applies each value at once and has no submit, so no summary. A product whose every check runs in the app may still choose the live summary. No Windows page speaks of a list of errors: this use is the system's judgment.

After a failed submit, focus moves to the list of errors when the form shows one, each entry a link to its field, so people hear that errors occurred and reach each field from it; without a list, focus moves to the first field in error, as the WAI tutorial advises after submit and as user agents generally do when their own validation stops a submit. Focus moves, so the summary or the field is announced by the move itself: a message that takes focus is a change of context, not a status message, and needs no live region.

One hidden live region per form, aria-live="polite", present in the initial markup (a region added with its content may not be announced), filled with "Label: message" when an error or a warning appears on leaving a field, or a success when its check runs. Not role="alert" nor aria-live="assertive": both interrupt, and role="alert" with aria-live speaks twice with VoiceOver on iOS. The message also stays referenced by the control's aria-describedby.

The form's polite region serves both situations of 4.1.3: role="status", ARIA22's technique for the result of an action, is itself a polite live region, so a success goes through the same region as an error or a warning, with no second region. When an error clears, the region is not filled or emptied to say so: with the default aria-relevant (additions text) a removal is not announced, and removals are for important changes only.

After a failed submit, the error summary's title takes focus through focus(), with tabindex="-1" so that it can be focused without entering the tab order; without a summary, the first field in error takes focus. The HTML specification lets the user agent focus one of the invalid controls when its own validation stops a submit; a form that validates itself does it in its script.

A page the server sends back with errors focuses the error summary's title, or the only field in error, with the autofocus attribute, which applies to all elements, not just to form controls, and needs no script; the title keeps tabindex="-1", and one element per document carries the attribute. The browser empties its autofocus candidates when the document has a target element: a fragment in the URL of that page, the form's action or a redirect, cancels the focus move, so it carries none; a browser may also skip autofocus once people have shown, by typing, that they do not want focus to change. Screen readers take people to the autofocused element without announcing what comes before it: the summary's title says how many errors there are, then its entries follow.

A page the server sends back with errors starts its title element with the number of errors, "3 errors – Delivery details – Checkout", as the WAI tutorial uses the page title to indicate errors: screen reader users receive it as soon as the page loads, even when the main heading sits deep in the content. The page's own title follows the count, so the title still describes the page's topic or purpose. The count is one plural string per language, held by the product like the summary's title. A check in the browser or a live update of the summary loads no page, so the title stays as it is.

Apple asks apps to inform VoiceOver when visible content changes: post an accessibility announcement of "Label: message" for an error or a warning that appears on leaving a field and for a success when its check runs (AccessibilityNotification.Announcement, iOS 17 and macOS 14; on AppKit, announcementRequested), at low priority, never high, which interrupts other speech and cannot be interrupted. Apple's accessibility references do not define low and default; low is our choice for a message that must not cut off the field people reached. No Apple page says how a form's errors reach its screen reader or where focus goes: this API is the system's judgment.

Apple asks that all feedback be accessible, received whether people look away from the screen or use VoiceOver: a warning or a success a form shows is announced like an error, at the same low priority.

After a failed submit, post a layout-changed notification with the error summary as the element VoiceOver moves to (AccessibilityNotification.LayoutChanged, iOS 17 and macOS 14; UIAccessibility layoutChanged on UIKit), or set an accessibility focus state on it, which moves VoiceOver focus; without a summary, move focus to the first field in error with its focus state, as Apple's own focus state example does when people sign in with a field left empty, and post the layout-changed notification with that field. No Apple page says how a form's errors reach its screen reader or where focus goes: this API is the system's judgment.

A polite live region (liveRegion Polite, the mode for most changes; Assertive only for time-sensitive content) holds "Label: message" when an error or a warning appears on leaving a field, or a success when its check runs, while the field keeps its error semantics. No Android page says how a form's errors reach its screen reader or where focus goes: this API is the system's judgment.

After a failed submit, a FocusRequester requests focus for the error summary, or for the first field in error without one, from the submit's event callback. No Android page says that TalkBack follows a requested focus, or how to move TalkBack to an element that is not a control. No Android page says how a form's errors reach its screen reader or where focus goes: this API is the system's judgment.

On Windows, an element whose AutomationProperties.LiveSetting is Polite (non-interruptive) and whose name is "Label: message", raising its live region change when an error or a warning appears on leaving a field, or a success when its check runs. LiveSetting is the WinUI API for content that changes. No Windows page says how a form's errors reach its screen reader or where focus goes: this API is the system's judgment.

On Windows, after a failed submit, the error summary, or the first field in error without one, takes focus through its Focus method, with the focus state Programmatic. Windows' Forms page asks only to mark the fields with invalid input and to require a resubmit. No Windows page says how a form's errors reach its screen reader or where focus goes: this API is the system's judgment.

An app gets the server's answer on the same screen, with no page sent back: when it arrives with errors, focus moves as after any failed submit, to the error summary's title or to the only field in error, with the means each platform's guideline names (a layout-changed notification or a focus state on iOS and macOS, a FocusRequester on Android, the Focus method with the focus state Programmatic on Windows). No Apple, Android or Windows page says where focus goes after a failed submit: this is the system's judgment.

Apple asks for a useful title for each window, one that helps people confirm their location and stays concise: on iOS and macOS, a screen's or a window's title keeps naming where people are after a failed submit, with no count of errors, and the focused error summary gives the count. No Apple page speaks of errors in a title: this is the system's judgment.

Android Developers names a window-like pane with paneTitle semantics, so that accessibility services can represent its changes: on Android, a screen or a pane keeps its title after a failed submit, with no count of errors, and the focused error summary gives the count. No Android page speaks of errors in a title: this is the system's judgment.

The Windows title bar identifies the app with its icon and title and may show other information such as a document's title: on Windows, the title keeps naming the app and what is open after a failed submit, with no count of errors, and the focused error summary gives the count. No Windows page speaks of errors in a title: this is the system's judgment.
Validate fields when it makes sense: an email address when people move to another field, a user name or password before they leave it; show errors right next to the field.
Make sure people understand that they must provide the required data before they can continue, for example by enabling the Next or Continue button only once the required fields are filled in.
Expose an error with the error semantics of the field, so the screen reader reads the error with it; announce content that changes without focus with a polite live region.

Material gives a text field's error text an alert role, so it is announced when it appears, on its own, without the field's label: a message that relies on its label then does not say which field it concerns. Focused, the field reads its error with it through its error semantics, and an error summary names the field in each entry; no source gives a way to add the label to the announcement itself.
Error identification, labels or instructions and error suggestion apply to non-web software as they do to web content.

On the web, the label of most fields sits immediately before the field, above it or to its left (to its right or above it in a right-to-left language), and the label of a checkbox or a radio after it; labels above the fields reduce horizontal scrolling for people who zoom and on small screens.

On Android, Material's text field label sits inside the container, in the middle while the field is empty and at its top once the field is selected or filled, always visible; a separate adjacent label aligned to the container's leading edge may take its place.
Apple gives no rule on where a text field's label sits; because a placeholder disappears when people start typing, a separate label describing the field can be useful.
On macOS, a checkbox typically has its title on its trailing side, and a radio button is followed by its label.

In a label column, each label sits immediately before its field: aligned to the end of the column, 12 px from the control, to the left of the field in a left-to-right language and to the right in a right-to-left one, so a screen magnifier finds it next to the field and no label can be taken for its neighbour's.

A label column stacks its labels above their fields when the form is too narrow for a label and its control side by side, by default under 30 rem of the form's own width, so the form reflows at a width of 320 CSS px without scrolling in two dimensions. A product that keeps the column at smaller widths still has to meet that.
On the web the form is a size container and a container query on its own width stacks the labels, with no script: it stacks in a narrow panel on a wide screen as on a phone, and at 400 % zoom.
On iOS, horizontally adjacent views may need to stack vertically at larger Dynamic Type sizes to give text more room: a label column stacks at the largest text sizes, whatever the form's width.

On Windows, labels are left-aligned and placed above the input control, many controls having a Header property for it; a form with labels on the left is shown as what not to do, so a form's labelPlacement stays above on Windows.

On the web, the form marks the fewer fields: "(optional)" in the label or legend of each optional field, with a note before the first field saying the others are required, when most fields are required; "(required)" in the label or legend of each required field when most are optional. A required control keeps the required attribute either way.

On the web, a "(required)" mark is hidden from assistive technology (aria-hidden), because the required attribute already exposes the state and the parenthetical may stay out of the accessible name; an "(optional)" mark stays in the label's text, so it is part of the accessible name, because no attribute exposes that a field is optional. Each fact is said once.

On Android, each required field ends its label with an asterisk, as Material asks; the asterisk is explained once, in supporting text or in a note before the first field, and the accessibility label includes it.
On Windows, each required field ends its label with an asterisk, explained once before the first field, and sets AutomationProperties.IsRequiredForForm so assistive technology knows it is required.
On iOS and macOS, Apple gives no mark for a required field, so the generic rule applies: "(optional)" with a note, or "(required)" when most fields are optional.

On macOS, a required control sets accessibilityRequired, so VoiceOver knows it is required and a visible "(required)" is hidden from it; on iOS, no accessibility trait says required, so "(required)" stays in the accessibility label. Each fact is said once.

Fields stand far enough apart that each label reads as its own control's: 16 px between two fields, more than the space between a field's label and its control, so the label stays visually close to and distinct from its control and is not taken for the field above.

Groups of fields stand further apart than fields: 32 px between two groups, and a group's title 12 px above its first field, so the space shows where a group ends and which fields its title introduces. The grouping is also carried in the code, a fieldset and its legend on the web, never by the space alone.

A field's label sits 6 px above its control, nearer to it than to anything else: its own description and message 6 px under it, the next field 16 px away. In a group, the options sit 4 px apart and 6 px from the legend or description above them, so the legend reads as the title of the whole list and each option as one target.
On iOS, each option of a checkbox or radio group reaches Apple's 44 x 44 pt hit region as a row at least 44 pt tall, 4 pt from the next; the other gaps of a field and a group stay as on the web.

On Android, Material's Checkbox and RadioButton set a 48 dp minimum themselves when they can receive actions: each option row is at least 48 dp tall, 4 dp from the next; the other gaps stay as on the web.

On Windows, the Forms page spaces individual input controls 24 px apart and groups of input controls 48 px apart; the design system keeps 16 px between fields and 32 px between groups of fields on every platform, Windows included: recorded differences, not platform values.
The fields of a form take keyboard focus in their reading order, on every platform, so the order keeps their meaning.

A form that is submitted has a submit button: Enter in a single-line field submits the form through its first submit button (implicit submission); a form without one and with two fields or more cannot be submitted with Enter. A search form whose only field is the Search field needs none: Enter submits it, with or without a button.

Enter submits from every single-line field and enterkeyhint changes only the key's label, so when a form sets it, it names the form's action (go, send, search, done) on every single-line field, never next.

Tabbing between fields moves in a logical sequence. Every field but the last shows the next return key and moves focus to the next field in its submit action (a focus state); the last field names the form's action (done, go, send, search) and submits the form.

Tab follows the order the fields appear in. Every field but the last sets the Next IME action, which moves focus to the next field by default; the last field sets the form's action (Done, Go, Send, Search) and submits the form.

On macOS, the key view loop follows the fields' reading order and Return in a field sends its action; on Windows, the tab order, by default the order the controls are added, follows the reading order.

decisions.text: The severity fill applies to the choice controls' empty boxes: an unchecked checkbox or radio box in error takes the subtle error fill, global.bg.subtle.functional.error.default (#FEECEA in light mode, #2B0B08 in dark mode), inside its error border, at rest and on hover alike; a checked or indeterminate box keeps its brand fill, so checked still reads checked. One rule for every control (forms-severity-fill). The border and the message carry the error; the tint is not the cue. The Checkbox, the Checkbox group and the Radio group carry it in a new component token, control.background.error.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 2b, point b3): B, tinted when empty, chosen over the recommended A, among: A, border only, the rule severity-fill saying it applies to field-like boxes (recommended: the tint is barely visible on a 16 to 20 px box); B, the subtle error fill inside an unchecked box (chosen); C, a checked box in error turns the error accent, Material's selected error (rejected: in dark mode the checked box falls to 3.74 down to 2.80:1 on levels 0 to 3, under the 3:1 of WCAG 1.4.11 on level 3, and a checked box should still read checked); D, B and C together. No words from the team beyond the choice. Measured from the resolved tokens: The error border on the fill 5.45:1 in light mode and 5.14:1 in dark mode (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1), on the surface levels 0 to 3 unchanged (6.12 / 5.79 / 6.12 / 5.79:1 light, 4.97 / 4.55 / 4.16 / 3.73:1 dark); the fill against the surface 1.12 / 1.06 / 1.12 / 1.06:1 light and 1.03 / 1.12 / 1.23 / 1.37:1 dark, decoration, not the cue.

decisions.text: A required Checkbox group means at least one option checked. No box carries the required state (the template stops putting it on the first box): on a checkbox it requires that very box, so on one box it asks for one given option and on every box for all of them, never one of several. The product checks the group when the form is submitted (forms-validation-timing) and shows its error in the group's message, "Choose at least one". On the web the legend's "(required)" is not hidden from assistive technology: no state says that a group is required, since aria-required is not supported on the group role a fieldset maps to, so the word is part of the group's name (the principle of forms-required-mark-exposure: hide the word only where a state says it). A set of consents that must all be accepted is a set of separate required Checkboxes. The Radio group is unchanged: a required radio makes its group required natively, and its legend's "(required)" stays hidden.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 2b, point b2): A, at least one, said in words, as recommended, among: A (chosen); B, aria-required on the fieldset with "(required)" hidden (rejected: aria-required is not supported on group, so "required" may never be said while the visible word is hidden); C, required on every box (rejected: the browser then asks for every option, "all", which the legend's "at least one" never means; consents that must all be accepted are separate Checkboxes); D, today, required on the first box only (rejected: a bug found in step 4 point 1, the browser blocks the submit until that one option is checked, even when another one is). No words from the team beyond the choice. Sources opened on 2026-11-27: WAI-ARIA 1.2 aria-required (Used in Roles), HTML Checkbox state and Radio Button state (constraint validation), HTML-AAM fieldset (group role), MDN input type checkbox (validation).

decisions.text: The Search field takes the Text field's severities: the severity property (none, error, warning, success; none by default), the message property and the message part under the description, and the severityIcon property (after-control, message, none; message by default), painted with the Text field's values (accent functional border, subtle functional fill, functional message and icon colors), so a required or checked search says a missing or wrong query in text next to the field, as every other text-entry control. It keeps required and the required mark; it differs from the Text field only by its search icon and its return key. A product uses only the severities its search needs.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 2b, point b1): A, the Text field's severities, as recommended, among: A, none, error, warning and success with a message and severityIcon (chosen); B, error only, like the choice controls (rejected: the step 5 reason for the choice controls, nothing to confirm or warn about, does not hold for a typed query, which can deserve a warning, and the field family would diverge); C, the Search field drops required and the mark, a search is never required (rejected: HTML lets a search input be required, and a search inside a form, such as finding a company, can be mandatory, so the product would have to swap components); D, today, required with no severity (rejected: an empty required search showed only the browser's own bubble, against the rules form-control and error-in-text, WCAG 3.3.1). No words from the team beyond the choice. Sources opened on 2026-11-27: MDN input type search (making input required).

decisions.text: By default a label column stacks, every label back above its field, when the form itself is narrower than 30 rem (480 px): on the web with a container query on the form, no script, so it stacks wherever the form sits (a page, a dialog, a side panel) and at 400 % zoom. A product may keep the column at smaller widths, or move the threshold, when its labels and controls still fit; it stays bound by reflow, no scrolling in two dimensions at a width of 320 CSS px. iOS and Android also stack it at the largest text sizes; Windows keeps its labels above (forms-label-column).
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-27 (#105 step 10, point 8): A, the form's own width, as the recommended default, among: A, when the form is narrower than 30 rem, a container query (chosen); B, when the viewport is narrower than 600 px, a media query (rejected: a form in a narrow side panel on a wide screen keeps its column and squeezes its controls); C, never by itself, left to the product (rejected as the default: at 320 px the controls get a few characters or the page scrolls sideways, against 1.4.10). The team's words: "Step 10.8 -> A as a recommendation, but in the end it'll always depend on the product constraints, maybe we could have forms that stay horizontal even at really small breakpoints (not the majority of cases but it can happen)." Hence the default with a product override, the team's principle (a default, each platform's guidance, the product's constraints), the override still bound by 1.4.10. C38, a sufficient technique for 1.4.10, changes a label and its input to a vertical alignment "when space is limited"; Understanding 1.4.10 asks for content at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels without scrolling in two dimensions; HIG Layout (Adaptability) says horizontally adjacent views may need to stack vertically at larger Dynamic Type sizes, and #103 step 20 found a label beside its control must stack at the largest text sizes on iOS and Android (WCAG 1.4.4). The 30 rem threshold is the system's judgment: a 14 em label column, the 12 px gap and a control of about 240 px; no source gives a number. Sources opened on 2026-11-27: C38, Understanding 1.4.10, HIG Layout (Adaptability).

decisions.text: The space between a label column and its controls is a fourth semantic addition owned by the Forms foundation, form.gap.label-column → {space.12}, next to form.gap.field, form.gap.group and form.gap.title (forms-gap-tokens). It is its own token, not an alias of form.gap.title: a group's title introduces the fields under it, a label in the column names the control beside it, so the two may diverge though they share 12 px today. The same on every platform; a platform may override it in its overlay, and none does.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-27 (#105 step 10, point 7b), asked on its own after point 7: A, no addition, the rule naming space.12 (rejected); B, a fourth semantic addition form.gap.label-column → {space.12} (recommended, chosen). The team's words: "B, add the token"; the choice is the approval this addition needs, as no semantic token beyond the Figma library is added without asking, and nothing else is added. Like the three gaps of point 4, a semantic token lets a platform override the value, reaches Figma and Penpot as a variable, and is what a form's layout reads. The 12 px follows point 7 (forms-label-alignment); Windows' Spacing page gives 12 epx between a control and its label (a design page outside the trusted sources, named here only).

decisions.text: In a label column (labelPlacement start, forms-label-column), every label and every group legend aligns to the end of the column, against its control: the column is as wide as the longest label, at most 14 em, and each label ends 12 px (space.12) from its control whatever the other labels' lengths. A label's first line is centred on the control's box; the description and the message stay under the control; right-to-left mirrors start and end. Windows keeps its labels above (forms-label-column). The ragged start edge of the labels is the trade-off.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-27 (#105 step 10, point 7): B, as recommended, among: A, labels at the start of the same fitted column (rejected: a short label ends far from its control when another label is long, 80 px or more on the sheet); B, labels at the end of the column, against the control (chosen); C, labels at the start of a fixed 160 px column (rejected: too wide for short labels, long ones wrap). The team's words: "Step 10.7 -> B". G162 positions labels "immediately before the field", to the left (or the right in a right-to-left language) or above, which also "makes labels easier to locate with a screen magnifier"; RGAA test 11.4.2 asks the label to be visually "accolée immédiatement" above or to the left of its field (to the right in right-to-left), and its glossary defines "accolés" as visually close enough that the relation cannot be confused, with no distance. Fixed on every option: the first line centred on the box (step 3 point 4 measured a field lining up with a Button of the same size that way), 12 px between the column and the control, the description and the message under the control. Whether the 12 px becomes a semantic addition is point 7b. iOS and Android have no page on label alignment: the default applies where a product uses a label column. Sources opened on 2026-11-27: G162, RGAA criterion 11.4 (tests 11.4.2 and 11.4.3), RGAA glossary (accolés).
