decisions.text: The form sets where its labels sit, never a field: a form setting, labelPlacement (above by default, start), set once per form and passed to every field-like control of the form, as markedFields is (forms-marked-fields), so a form never mixes placements. With start, the form sizes one shared label column for all its fields; a group's legend sits in that column; a checkbox, a radio or a switch keeps its label after the box. A design tool keeps the setting out of the component's variants, as markedFields. On Windows the labels stay above, its own guidance. How the labels align in the column and when it stacks are points 7 and 8 of step 10.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 10, point 6): A, as recommended, among: A, the form, a form setting like markedFields with one shared column (chosen); B, each field, a fixed 160 px label column (rejected: two fields could disagree, and a fixed column cuts long labels or wastes room on short ones); C, the form with a per-field override (rejected: the override brings back the mixed placements A avoids). No words from the team beyond the choice. It completes step 3 point 4 (forms-label-placement), which left the column and whether a field exposes the placement to this step. On the web the sheet built the shared column with one CSS grid and each field a subgrid row, no script; a group's fieldset needs its legend in that column (the sheet used display: contents, which may drop a fieldset's group semantics in some engines: to check before the field family builds it). Windows Forms places labels above the input control and shows labels on the left as a Don't. The field-side work (the labelPlacement property on the field family's templates and Figma blueprints) is built with the field family. Sources opened on 2026-11-27: Windows Forms (Labels).

decisions.text: Every form control spaces its parts 6 px apart (space.6): a field's label → control → description → message; a group's legend → options when it has no description, description → options, options → message. A group's description sits right under its legend (0 px), the two reading as one heading, and its options stack 4 px apart (space.4; 16 px in the horizontal orientation). The Text field family keeps its 6 px (#103 step 5); the Select moves 4 → 6, the Checkbox group and the Radio group 8 → 6 between their parts and 8 → 4 between options, and their legend takes the row gap as its bottom margin (it touched its next part before). These are component tokens, the same on every platform: on iOS each option row is at least 44 pt tall, on Android 48 dp, both 4 apart; macOS keeps the web's values; Windows' own spacing is a recorded difference. iOS's 44 pt rows are a guideline, not a token: component tokens never fork per platform.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 10, point 5): D, the team's own proposal for the web, chosen over the recommended A once the sheet showed it. The team's words: "We'd like to try this instead on the web: Label and field: 6px; Field and description: 6px; Group name and group description: 0px; Group elements between themselves (radios, checkbox): 4px; Group elements and message (severity): 6px", then, on the three values the proposal left open (description → options 6, legend → options 6 without a description, a field's description → message 6): "Yes, D as assumed, and deduce what's expected for the other platforms". Rejected: today (6 / 4 / 8 and a legend at 0 px, a bug), A (6 everywhere, options 8 apart; recommended), B (fields 6, groups 8), C (8 everywhere, reopening #103 step 5). Measured on the web: medium options 24 px tall, 28 apart; small 21 px tall, 25 apart, so WCAG 2.5.8's spacing exception (a 24 px circle on each undersized target) passes by 1 px. Platforms, deduced from their own guidance: iOS, HIG Accessibility (Mobility) gives 44 x 44 pt, and at a 28 pt pitch an option's hit region cannot reach over its neighbours as a field's does (#103 step 18), so the rows grow to 44 pt; Android, Material's Checkbox and RadioButton set 48 dp themselves (Compose accessibility defaults); macOS, HIG gives a 20 x 20 pt minimum (28 by default), which the 21 and 24 pt rows meet; Windows, Spacing and gutters gives 8 epx between a control and its header and 12 epx between a control and its label, and Alignment, margin and padding asks for increments of 4 epx (design pages outside the trusted sources, cited in the rationale only): 6 differs, recorded, and a Windows product may override it (forms-platform-gaps). Sources opened on 2026-11-27: HIG Accessibility (Mobility), Compose accessibility defaults (minimum target sizes), Understanding 2.5.8, Windows Spacing and gutters.

decisions.text: The gaps of a form are three semantic tokens, additions to the semantic tier owned by the Forms foundation: form.gap.field → {space.16} between two fields (forms-field-gap), form.gap.group → {space.32} between two groups of fields and form.gap.title → {space.12} between a group's title and its first field (forms-group-gap). The actions take form.gap.field or form.gap.group, whichever precedes them (forms-actions-gap), with no token of their own. The values are the same on every platform; a platform may override them in its overlay, and none does (Windows' 24 and 48 px stay recorded differences).
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 10, point 4): B, as recommended, among: A, no token, the rule naming the space.* steps (rejected: no platform could override them, and Figma binds the layout to bare scale steps); B, semantic additions form.gap.field, form.gap.group and form.gap.title (recommended, chosen; the team's choice is the approval these additions need, as no semantic token beyond the Figma library is added without asking); C, component tokens of a Form component (rejected: there is no Form component, and component tokens are never overridden per platform). No words from the team beyond the choice. A semantic token lets a platform override the default (Windows states 24 and 48 px: a separate decision, not taken), is exported as a Figma and a Penpot variable through the token build, and is what a product's form layout reads (the screens' form stacks). The Spacing foundation's rule layout, which said there were no layout tokens, now names them.

decisions.text: A form's actions (its submit button and the buttons next to it) take the gap of what precedes them: space.16 (the field gap, forms-field-gap) after a form without groups, space.32 (the group gap, forms-group-gap) after a grouped form. The buttons stand space.8 (8 px) apart. No value of its own, on every platform.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 10, point 3): C, as recommended, among: A, always the field gap, 16 px (rejected: in a grouped form the buttons sit 16 px under the last group but 32 px under the groups before it, so they read as part of the last group); B, always space.24, between the field and the group gap (rejected: a third value to learn, still less than the group gap); C, the gap of what precedes (recommended, chosen). No words from the team beyond the choice. The actions submit the whole form, not its last group: after groups they stand apart as a group does, in a plain form they are one more row. No trusted page states the space before a form's buttons: Windows Forms' one-column sample puts Save at its field gap (Margin="0,24"), and Windows Spacing and gutters gives 8 epx between buttons, the 8 px kept between the actions (a design page outside the trusted sources, cited in the rationale only). The screens already do it: their sign-in forms put the submit button 16 px under the last field and space their button rows 8 px apart. Sources opened on 2026-11-27: Windows Forms (Spacing, one-column form sample), Windows Spacing and gutters.

decisions.text: On the web, a page the server sends back with errors starts its title with the count: "3 errors – " then the page's own title ("1 error – …" with one), from one plural string per language the product holds, like the summary's title. After a check in the browser or the app, or a live update of the summary (forms-summary-updates), no page is loaded and the title stays; the focused summary gives the count. iOS, Android and desktop keep their screen or window title (Apple's window titles, Android's pane titles, the Windows title bar), the focused summary giving the count; no platform page speaks of errors in a title, so this is the system's judgment. No component, token or rendering change here; the component is built in #129.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-27 (#105 step 9, point 6b-2): A, as recommended, among: A, the count first, "3 errors – Delivery details – Checkout", "1 error – …" with one, the product's plural string (recommended, chosen); B, "Error: Delivery details – Checkout", a word without the count, the pattern of a government design system outside the trusted sources (rejected); C, the summary's title as the prefix, "There are 3 errors in this form – …", reusing point 3's string (rejected: long, the page's name cut in narrow tabs); D, the title unchanged (rejected). The team's words: "Step 9.6b-2 -> A". A title names where people are; only a web page sent back by the server is a new page, so only that page's title carries the count, while a check in the browser, a live update or any app screen keep their title and let the focused summary say the count. Sources opened on 2026-11-27: the WAI forms tutorial, using the page title ("3 Errors – Billing Address"; screen reader users receive the feedback as soon as the page loads) and using the main heading; Understanding 2.4.2, intent (titles describe topic or purpose and identify the current location); Apple's HIG Toolbars, titles (a useful title for each window helps people confirm their location; concise, under 15 characters); Android Developers' Compose semantics, window-like components (paneTitle); Windows' Title bar (it identifies the app via its icon and title, and may show a document's title). None of the platform pages speaks of errors in a title.

decisions.text: Two groups of fields, sections of a form with their own title, are space.32 (32 px) apart, from the bottom of a group's last field to the next group's title, and a group's title sits space.12 (12 px) above its first field. A Checkbox group or a Radio group is one control and takes the field gap (forms-field-gap). The values hold on every platform: Windows' own guidance, groups of input controls 48 px apart, is recorded as a difference, not a platform value.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 10, point 2): A, as recommended, among: A, groups space.32 apart, twice the 16 px between fields as Windows doubles its own (24 to 48), a title space.12 above its first field (recommended, chosen); B, groups space.48 apart, Windows' value, three times the field gap on 16 px fields, title 12 (rejected); C, a Divider with 16 px on each side, title 12 (rejected: a line more to draw, a divider being a choice a product can add over A). No words from the team beyond the choice. The title is closer to its fields (12) than they are to each other (16) and than to the group above (32), so it reads as theirs. No trusted source gives a value: Windows Forms gives 48 px with controls 24 px apart; HIG Layout groups related items with negative space, container shapes or separator lines; the WAI forms tutorial says grouping is carried out visually and in the code (a fieldset and its legend). Sources opened on 2026-11-27: Windows Forms (Spacing), HIG Layout (Visual hierarchy), WAI forms tutorial (grouping controls).

decisions.text: Two fields of a form are space.16 (16 px) apart, at every field size, from the bottom of a field's last part (control, description or message) to the next field's label; a Checkbox group and a Radio group are one field each. The value holds on every platform: Windows' own guidance, input controls 24 px apart, is recorded as a difference, not a platform value.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 10, point 1): A, chosen over the recommended B, among: A, space.16 at every field size, the value of the screens' stack today (chosen); B, space.24 at every field size, Windows' "should be spaced 24px apart", the only value a trusted page gives (recommended, rejected); C, by field size, 16 / 20 / 24 px for small / medium / large fields (rejected: a form mixing sizes has no single rhythm, three values to keep in step). No words from the team beyond the choice. No W3C source gives a value: the WAI forms tutorial asks for a close and distinct visual relationship between a label and its control, and HIG Text fields asks to leave enough space between fields that people see which field belongs with each label. With 6 px between a field's own parts (#103 step 5), the next label stands more than twice as far from the field above as from its own control. From #103 step 18: any space of 10 px or more between fields keeps the iOS and Android hit regions of two fields apart, so 16 needs nothing more. Sources opened on 2026-11-27: Windows Forms (Spacing), HIG Text fields (Best practices), WAI forms tutorial (visual position of label text).

decisions.text: On the web, a page the server sends back with errors focuses the error summary's title, or the only field in error, with the HTML autofocus attribute, no script: the title keeps tabindex="-1" and carries autofocus. Its limit: no fragment in the URL of that page (the form's action or a redirect), since the browser skips autofocus when the document has a target element. iOS, Android and desktop get the server's answer on the same screen and move focus with the means already decided (forms-focus-after-submit) once it arrives. The error count in the page's title is point 6b-2. No component, token or rendering change here; the component is built in #129.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 9, point 6b-1): A, as recommended, among: A, the autofocus attribute on the summary's title (tabindex="-1") or on the only field's control, no script (recommended, chosen); B, a script that calls focus() on load (rejected); C, no focus move, the page read from the top (rejected). The team's words: "Step 9.6b-1 -> A". It follows the native-first principle of point 4: no script on the web where the browser gives the same result. Checked on 2026-11-26 with pages that send themselves back (a GET to themselves) in Chromium 156 and WebKit 27.2 (Playwright) and Firefox 161 (WebDriver BiDi): autofocus on a tabindex=-1 heading focuses it on load and after a submit in all three, also after following an entry link and submitting, the submit URL dropping the fragment; loaded with a fragment naming an element, nothing is focused in all three, as the HTML standard says; B's focus() at the end of the body does the same, except with such a fragment, where Chromium and WebKit lose the focus and Firefox keeps it. Screen readers were not recorded. Focus scrolls the title only until it shows, which can leave the entries below the fold: a separate finding, not part of this decision. Sources opened on 2026-11-27: HTML, the autofocus attribute (it applies to all elements; the autofocus candidates are emptied when the top document has a target element; a browser may skip it once the user indicated, for example by typing, that focus should not change; one per autofocus scoping root), MDN autofocus (the element the fragment names wins; screen readers "teleport" people to the element without announcing what comes before it).

decisions.text: The error summary shows the errors of the last submit: fixing a field does not change it; each submit rebuilds it (count, entries) and focuses its title, removes it when one error is left (focus to that field) or when none is (the form is sent). This is the default on every platform, whoever checks the values. A product whose every check runs in the browser or in the app may update it live instead: an entry leaves when its field is fixed, the title's count follows and is announced politely (WCAG 4.1.3), the summary goes when no entry is left, at the cost of script on every field; never when a check waits for the server. On iOS and macOS, Apple's guidance to verify values as soon as people enter them leads a form whose every check runs in the app to the live summary, its new title announced at low priority; on Android, Android Developers' check as people type does the same, the new title in a polite live region; on Windows, the marked fields and the resubmit of its Forms page are the default; on iOS, macOS and Windows the summary never lists empty required fields, their submit being disabled until those are filled. No Apple, Android or Windows page speaks of a list of errors: each platform's use is the system's judgment. The web's page sent back by the server is point 6b. No component, token or rendering change here; the component is built in #129.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 9, point 6a): D, a default with a product override, added in discussion and chosen over the recommended A, among: A, updated at each submit only (recommended): fixing a field clears its error silently and leaves the summary as it is until the next submit rebuilds it; B, updated live: an entry leaves when its field is fixed, the title's count follows and is announced politely, the summary goes when no entry is left; C, updated live, the fixed entry kept and marked fixed with no link, the title and its count waiting for the next submit (rejected); D, A by default, B as a product override when every check runs in the browser or the app, never when a check waits for the server (chosen). In discussion, the team noted that on the web the summary can follow the fields live when the browser is the validator, but that once the form goes to the server only a resubmit tells whether a field is fixed. The team's words on the choice: "Step 9.6a -> D. Also, remember it's an agnostic guideline as well. We 'know the answer' only for the web. You'll need to deduce the Android, iOS, Windows, etc. guidelines from their own guidance/resources." The team's principle, which D applies: "We enforce default principles, the platforms follow their own guidance, and the product can still override at the end with their specificities." So the platforms are deduced from what each says about when a value is checked: Apple asks to verify values as soon as people enter them; Android Developers validates a field as people type and when people move to the next field; Windows marks the invalid controls on submission and requires a resubmit, and its instantly updating forms have no submit. A mixed form, with some checks in the app and one on the server, would be half live and half stale, hence never live when a check waits for the server. Sources opened on 2026-11-27: SCR32 (the list built in the submit handler; an existing list replaced "with the new lot"), the WAI forms tutorial, overall feedback and listing errors (feedback when a form is submitted; nothing on updating the list while people fix fields), Understanding 4.1.3, modification of status text (a status text that persists and changes is usually a new status message), Apple's HIG Entering data, Android Developers' quick guide Validate input as the user types and its keyboard action logic, Windows' Forms page (instantly updating, submitting with button).

decisions.text: The error summary sits at the top of the form, inside it: after the form's heading and introduction, before the first field; in a dialog or a panel, at the top of that form. Its title is a heading one level below the form's heading (or the page's when the form has none). On iOS, Android and desktop, it is the first element of the form's scrolling content, scrolling with it, never pinned (the system's judgment: no platform page says where). No component, token or rendering change here; the component is built in #129.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 9, point 5): A, as recommended, among: A, at the top of the form, before its first field (chosen); B, at the top of the page, under its main heading, before the form (rejected: written for a page that is only the form; in a dialog the top of the page is behind it, and with other content or other forms it sits away from the form it lists); C, at the end of the form, above the submit button (rejected: read after the fields it lists, Tab from its last entry goes to submit, no source places it there). No words from the team beyond the choice. On a page that is only the form, A is the place the WAI tutorial ("list them at the top of the page, before the form") and G139 ("a text description at the top of the page") give; SCR32 displays the list "at the top of the form", its container inside the form before the first fieldset. Before the fields, the reading sequence (1.3.2) and the focus order (2.4.3) follow the meaning: the live sheet checked that Tab after the last entry reaches the first field in A, the page's links first in B, and submit in C. Placing it needs no script in any option (the team's native-first principle of point 4). Sources opened on 2026-11-26: the WAI forms tutorial (listing errors), G139, SCR32, Understanding 1.3.2 and 2.4.3 (intents); Apple's HIG Entering data, Material and Windows say nothing of a list of errors.

decisions.text: The error summary lists the errors only, one entry per field in error, in the form's order; warnings stay under their fields. On the web, each entry is a plain in-page link, no JavaScript: <a href="#field-id">, to the field's control, and for a group to its first option, never to the fieldset; each field's control carries a CSS scroll-margin-top so its label, or its group's legend, stays visible above the focused control. Each activation adds a URL fragment and a history entry (Back walks the fields first), and a single-page app whose router takes over # links may need its own handling, the product's choice. iOS, Android and desktop move focus to the field with the means of forms-focus-after-submit. No component, token or rendering change here: the scroll margin is built on the field controls with the Error summary component in #129.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 9, point 4): B+, an option raised in discussion, chosen over the recommended A. The team's words: "the reason would be to use native approaches at first, so for the web not relying on extra JavaScript if we can". Native first: on the web the browser already focuses the target of a fragment link, and CSS scroll-margin-top keeps the label in view, so script adds nothing. Among: A, errors only, a link plus a few lines of script that focus the control and scroll its label into view (recommended; not chosen: the same result with script); B, errors only, a plain link and nothing more (superseded by B+: the label is cut off at the top edge, and a link to a fieldset focuses nothing); B+, B with scroll-margin-top on the controls and group links to their first option (chosen); C, errors then warnings under "Also check" (rejected); D, errors and warnings in one list (rejected). Verified on 2026-11-26 with a probe page in Chromium 156, WebKit 27.2 (Playwright 1.64) and Firefox 161 (WebDriver BiDi): following each link focuses the control; without a margin the control lands at the top (label 22 to 24 px above the view); with scroll-margin-top 40 px the label shows 16 to 18 px from the top and a legend 9 to 11 px; a link to a group's first radio or checkbox focuses it; a link to the fieldset focuses nothing; each activation adds one history entry and Back returns to the previous fragment. Sources opened on 2026-11-26: HTML, scrolling to a fragment (scroll into view with block "start", then the focusing steps, the viewport as the fallback) and navigate to a fragment (a push adds a history entry); CSS Scroll Snap Module Level 1, scroll-margin (on fragment navigation and scrollIntoView the UA uses the scroll snap area, even when snapping is off; not in the trusted sources, so cited here only); MDN scroll-margin-top; the WAI forms tutorial, listing errors, and G139.

decisions.text: The error summary's title is a statement with the count: "There are 3 errors in this form", one sentence with no period (forms-message-punctuation), the number being the number of entries. The Error summary component holds it as its English default, and the product passes its own string, translated and pluralised: one plural string per language, its form picked by the language's plural rules from the number, never a number joined to a word. The title states and the entries say the fix (forms-message-says-the-fix, forms-message-relies-on-label): the title is not a message. It replaces the provisional example "Check 2 fields" of forms-focus-after-submit. No component, token or rendering change here; the component is built in #129.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 9, point 3), B chosen over the recommended A, among: A, "Check 3 fields", the count and the fix in two words (recommended; not chosen); B, "There are 3 errors in this form", a statement with the count, the WAI tutorial's own example heading (chosen); C, "Check these fields", the fix without a count (rejected); D, "The form has errors", as G139's "Errors have occurred", no count (rejected). No words from the team beyond the choice. Fit with step 11: the rule that a message says the fix applies to the entries, each "Label: message"; the title only states how many there are, so the two do not conflict, and the title follows the punctuation rule (one sentence, no period). Plurals: English has two forms (one, other) and Arabic six (zero, one, two, few, many, other), so a translated title is one plural string chosen from the number (MDN Intl.PluralRules), not a fixed word after a number. Sources opened on 2026-11-26: the WAI forms tutorial, listing errors (example heading "There are 2 errors in this form"), SCR32 ("N Errors in Submission"), G139 (example 3, "Errors have occurred"), MDN Intl.PluralRules.

decisions.text: A dedicated Error summary component renders a form's error summary: not the Alert, not a variant of the Alert, and not a pattern built from other components. It has no alert role, its title takes focus after a failed submit (forms-focus-after-submit), and its entries are links to their fields (forms-message-relies-on-label). Its behaviour (title and count, entries, place, updates and clearing) is decided in #105 step 9 points 3 to 6; the component is built in its own pull request after this foundation (#129). No component, token or rendering change here.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 9, point 2), C chosen as recommended, among: A, the Alert as it is (rejected: it carries role="alert" and never moves focus, while the summary's title takes focus; the APG Alert pattern says alerts must not affect keyboard focus, and WAI-ARIA 1.2 says to use alertdialog instead of alert when focus moves to a message); B, a summary variant of the Alert (rejected: one component with two roles and two focus contracts, and the validator requires role="alert" on every Alert rendering); C, a new Error summary component (chosen); D, a Forms pattern with no component (rejected: nothing would carry its tokens, template or Figma drawing). Sources opened on 2026-11-26: APG Alert pattern, WAI-ARIA 1.2 alert role.

decisions.text: An error summary is optional, never mandatory. By default, a form shows one after a failed submit when two fields or more are in error; with one error it shows none, and focus moves to the field in error (forms-focus-after-submit). A product may decide never to show one, typically a short form such as a sign-in with an email and a password: the explicit product override of the default (forms-platform-gaps). When a summary is shown, the rules already decided apply: its title takes focus after a failed submit (forms-focus-after-submit), its entries are "Label: message" as links to their fields (forms-message-relies-on-label), the announcements stay as they are (forms-error-announcement, forms-warning-success-announcement), and its rendering is decided by step 9 points 2 to 6. No source gives a threshold: the WAI tutorial, G139 and SCR32 list any number of errors, and Understanding 3.3.1 mandates no particular way, so WCAG is met with or without a summary. After people fix one of two errors and submit again, the summary goes and focus moves to the remaining field. The default holds on every platform: no Apple, Android or Windows page says whether a form lists its errors. No component, token or rendering change.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 9, point 1), C chosen, among: A, never a summary by default (rejected); B, a summary after every failed submit, whatever the number of errors, a one-field form excepted (recommended, rejected); C, a summary from two errors (chosen); D, no default, the product decides (rejected: it goes against the step 8 point 4 principle, a default the product may override). The team's words: "By default we'd recommend having summary only when there are more than 1 error (option C), but product can still decide to never have a summary. If there's a summary displayed, it should follow the rules we already have defined (for a11y, rendering, focus order). Summary is a possibility, it's optional, and not mandatory. For some cases, it's useless, like a login/password, or really short forms, etc." The threshold is the team's: no source gives one. Sources opened on 2026-11-26: WAI forms tutorial (listing errors), G139, SCR32, Understanding 3.3.1.

decisions.text: Where a platform has its own guidance, the form follows it; where it has none, the generic behaviour applies through the API the platform guideline names, and that API is the system's judgment. The rule announcement states this principle once, as the rule required already does, and every Apple, Android and Windows guideline that rests on an API alone (announcing an error, moving focus after a failed submit) ends with the same sentence: "No <Platform> page says how a form's errors reach its screen reader or where focus goes: this API is the system's judgment." Apple's low priority keeps its own caveat: the API is Apple's, only the level is the system's choice. The default is the rule; a product may still depart from it for its own specifics. No component, token or rendering change.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 8, point 4), B chosen as recommended, among: A, the five wordings stay ("chosen as our judgment", "this is our judgment", "these are our judgment", "low is our choice", "the system's judgment") (rejected: one fact said five ways, and the Android announcement guideline said nothing of its gap); B, one principle in the rule and one closing sentence on each API-only platform guideline (chosen); C, the APIs as examples and the means left to the product (rejected: two products on one platform could differ); D, as B plus a structured guideline field (basis: "judgment") shown by the site and checked by the validator (rejected for this step: it changes the schemas, the validator and the site for every spec, beyond the Forms foundation; filed as an issue). The team's principle: "We enforce default principles, the platforms follow their own guidance, and the product can still override at the end with their specificities." The override is explicit: a product may deviate for its own specifics, but the default is the rule.

decisions.text: After a failed submit, focus moves to the title of the form's error summary when the form has one, so people hear the count ("Check 2 fields") and every entry, "Label: message", as links to their fields (forms-message-relies-on-label); without a summary, focus moves to the first field in error. Focus moves once per submit and the move announces the summary or the field, with no live region. Per platform: on the web, focus() on the summary's title with tabindex="-1"; on iOS and macOS, a layout-changed notification with the summary, or an accessibility focus state, and for a field its focus state with the layout-changed notification; on Android, a FocusRequester; on Windows, Focus with the focus state Programmatic. Whether a form shows a summary, and from how many errors, is step 9, which must let the summary take focus. No component, token or rendering change.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 8, point 3), B chosen as recommended, among: A, focus always moves to the first field in error (rejected: with a summary, its count and its entries are never heard, and a visible summary is skipped); B, focus moves to the summary's title when there is one, otherwise to the first field in error (chosen); C, focus stays on the submit button and a polite status message says "Check N fields: Label, Label" (rejected: people are left at the bottom of the form, a polite message can be missed, and a new count string needs plural forms in every language); D, focus moves to the first field and the count is announced politely (rejected: two announcements compete, and the count repeats the summary). The team follows the recommendation because it rests on screen-reader best practice, not on its own use of screen readers. Why B: G139 example 3 and SCR32 move focus to the list of errors, each entry linking to its field; without a list, the WAI tutorial advises focusing the first field in error after submit, which is also what user agents do: the HTML specification lets them focus an invalid control when their validation stops a submit, and Understanding 3.3.1 says they generally set focus back to the first field in error. A message that takes focus is a change of context, not a status message (Understanding 4.1.3, excepted examples), so no live region is needed. B holds whatever step 9 decides on the summary. No Apple, Android or Windows page says where focus goes after a failed submit (Windows' Forms page only asks to mark the invalid fields and require a resubmit), and no Android page says TalkBack follows a FocusRequester or how to move TalkBack to an element that is not a control: the platform means are our judgment. Sources opened on 2026-11-26: WAI forms tutorial (after submit, listing errors), G139, SCR32, Understanding 3.3.1, Understanding 4.1.3, HTML interactively validate the constraints, MDN tabindex, Apple AccessibilityNotification.LayoutChanged, UIKit layoutChanged, SwiftUI AccessibilityFocusState and FocusState, Compose change focus behavior, Windows programmatic focus navigation and Forms.

decisions.text: A warning shown as people leave a field, and a success from a check people cannot make themselves, shown when that check runs, are announced politely through the form's announcement of an error (forms-error-announcement), as the field's label, a colon, a space and the message ("Email address: Check the domain: did you mean example.com?", "Username: This one is available"). An error that clears as people type is silent. Every platform uses the means of forms-error-announcement: on the web the form's one polite live region, on iOS and macOS a low-priority announcement, on Android a polite live region, on Windows an element with LiveSetting Polite. No component, token or rendering change.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 8, point 2), B chosen as recommended, among: A, only errors are announced (rejected: a warning and a success that appear without focus are status messages, and leaving them silent fails 4.1.3, AA); B, a warning and a success announced politely as "Label: message", a cleared error silent (chosen); C, everything announced, including "Label: no error" when an error clears (rejected: no source asks for a cleared error to be announced, it talks over people's typing, and it needs a new string in every language); D, as B but the message alone while focus is in the field, as in the WAI tutorial's binary-messages example (rejected: a second string and a rule that depends on focus, and a check that answers late, after people tab away, would then lack its label). The team follows the recommendation because it rests on screen-reader best practice, not on its own use of screen readers. Why B: it meets 4.1.3 with one rule and one string, the error summary entry's: Understanding 4.1.3 lists a warning under situation B (ARIA19) and the result of an action under situation A (ARIA22, role=status, an implicitly polite and atomic live region), both status messages, so the form's polite region serves both. No source asks for a cleared error to be announced: WAI-ARIA 1.2 aria-relevant treats removals as irrelevant by default and keeps removals for important changes, to be used sparingly; people hear their own keystrokes, the field no longer reads as in error when they come back, and the submit checks again. Apple asks that all feedback be accessible, VoiceOver included (HIG Feedback). No Apple, Android or Windows page covers announcing a warning, a success or a cleared error: each platform keeps the means chosen for an error, as our judgment. Sources opened on 2026-11-26: Understanding 4.1.3 (techniques, situations A and B), ARIA19, ARIA22, WAI-ARIA 1.2 status and aria-relevant, WAI forms tutorial (binary messages), Apple HIG Feedback.

decisions.text: When an error appears as people leave a field, focus already on the next one, the form announces the field and the message, politely, as one string: the field's label, a colon, a space, then the message, the same string as the field's error summary entry (forms-message-relies-on-label). Web: one hidden polite live region per form, present in the initial markup, filled with that string. iOS and macOS: an accessibility announcement of it at low priority (AccessibilityNotification.Announcement, iOS 17 and macOS 14; AppKit announcementRequested). Android: a polite live region with it, the field keeping its error semantics. Windows: an element with LiveSetting Polite named with it. The form owns the region, as it owns the summary: no component, token or rendering change. The error is checked again at submit.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 8, point 1), C chosen as recommended, among: A, nothing is announced, the message is read only when people come back to the field (rejected: an error that appears without focus is a status message, and announcing nothing fails 4.1.3, AA); B, the message alone, politely (rejected: a message relies on its label, forms-message-relies-on-label, so alone it does not say which field it concerns, and 3.3.1 asks that the item in error be identified); C, the label and the message, politely (chosen); D, the label and the message, assertively. The team follows the recommendation because it rests on screen-reader best practice, not on its own use of screen readers. Why C: polite is the default every source asks for: WAI-ARIA 1.2 says authors should not use assertive unless the interruption is imperative, and that an assertive update may clear the speech queue, here the name of the field people just reached; MDN uses polite normally and assertive only for time-critical notifications; Compose asks for Polite in most cases and Assertive sparingly. It meets 4.1.3 (Understanding 4.1.3, situation B, a warning on the existence of an error, technique ARIA19) and 3.3.1 (it names the field), and it reuses the summary entry's string, so the two never disagree. Departure, stated honestly: the WAI forms tutorial's on-focus-change example puts its message in an assertive live region, read before the next field, and Material gives a text field's error text an alert role, both D. Caveats: Apple's Announcement page only says that a high priority interrupts other speech and cannot be interrupted; what low and default mean is defined only outside the trusted Apple references, so low is our judgment of the least intrusive level. Windows' Forms page says nothing on announcing errors (an earlier summary of this pull request said otherwise): LiveSetting Polite is the WinUI API for content that changes, as our judgment where Windows is silent. Sources opened on 2026-11-26: WAI notifications (on focus change, during typing), Understanding 4.1.3 (techniques), ARIA19, Understanding 3.3.1, WAI-ARIA 1.2 aria-live and alert, MDN live regions, Apple HIG VoiceOver (navigation), Apple AccessibilityNotification.Announcement, AppKit announcementRequested, Compose semantics (alerts and pop-ups, error components), WinUI LiveSetting and AutomationLiveSetting, Windows Forms.

decisions.text: Inline, a message relies on the label it sits under: it says the fix without repeating the field's name ("Include an @, as in name@example.com" under Email address, not "Enter an email address with an @"), consistent with forms-message-says-the-fix and forms-message-punctuation. An error summary entry is the field's label verbatim, without its required or optional mark, a colon, a space, then the message with its own casing, the whole entry a link to the field ("Country: Choose one"); an entry whose message is empty shows the label alone, still as a link. Whether there is a summary is step 9's; this only words its entries. Consequence on Android: Material gives the error text an alert role, announced on its own when it appears, so that announcement does not say which field it concerns; the field still reads its error with its label when focused (error semantics) and the summary names it, and no source gives a way to add the label to the announcement.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 11, point 4), B chosen over the recommended A, among: A, one sentence naming the thing asked, used both inline and in the summary (recommended, rejected); B, rely on the label inline, the summary adds it (chosen); C, the summary lists labels only (rejected: it says where, not what to fix); D, the summary has its own sentences (rejected: two strings per error that drift apart, the problem before the fix). The team's reason: the summary must always locate the error, even when the message is useless. A backend may return no message, or several identical ones (bare error codes); with A, the summary would show an empty bullet with no link, or identical entries with no context; with B, the label is always there. Sources: the WAI tutorial's inline message relies on its label ("Use the format MM/YYYY.") and its list of errors references each control's label with an in-page link; G139 asks for a link to each field in error and G83 for text identifying the omitted fields; Understanding 3.3.1 asks that the item in error be identified, which the label does inline and in the summary; ARIA19's live-region messages and Apple's Writing example name the thing asked, A's sources; ARIA21's inline message sits under its label. Material and Compose: see the consequence. Windows' Forms page is silent on wording and on a summary. Casing after the colon: Microsoft's style guide lowercases the word after a colon in a sentence, Apple's style guide capitalizes it when a complete sentence follows, Material's grammar page is silent; both are style guides outside the trusted accessibility sources, and no trusted source settles it, so the simpler choice is kept, the message's own casing: the summary changes nothing in the message, whatever its language or its source.

decisions.text: The submit button stays enabled while required fields are empty, so that submitting shows what is missing (forms-validation-timing); this is the generic rule, applied as is on the web and on Android. On iOS, macOS and Windows, whose guidance asks for it, the submit button is disabled until the required fields are filled, and Enter (Return) does not submit the form while it is disabled.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 7, point 3), C, among: A, always enabled everywhere (against Apple's and Windows' guidance); B, disabled until the required fields are filled everywhere (nothing says what is missing, and on the web the button leaves the tab order, Enter does not submit and the label is exempt from contrast); C. It follows the foundation's principle that a platform follows its own requirements where it has them and the generic rule where it has none (label-placement, forms-required-windows-name). Sources opened: HIG Entering data, Windows Forms (submitting with button), HTML implicit submission, APG focusability of disabled controls, MDN aria-disabled, WAI after submit, Understanding 3.3.1 and 1.4.3 (inactive components, whose example is this very button). Material says nothing.

decisions.text: A message or a description of one sentence takes no period ("Choose a country", "We send the receipt to this address"); with two or more sentences, every sentence ends with its period ("Enter at least 20 characters. You have entered 10."); a question keeps its question mark ("Check the domain: did you mean example.com?"). Each is in sentence case, one sentence and a second only when the fix needs it, about one line at the field's default width, two lines at most. Consequence: assistive technology gets the description and the message as one string, the text of every node aria-describedby names joined by a space, so the separate ids add no pause and a one-sentence description runs into the message when read ("…to this address Enter an email…"); the template does not mend it: with an icon, after the control or in the message, the icon's name ("Error") falls between the two, with severityIcon none nothing does.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 11, point 3) among: A, a sentence with its period on every message and description (recommended); B, Material's rule, no period on a single sentence, periods on two or more, a question keeps its mark (chosen); C, never a period. The length was the same in every option. Departure from A's sources, recorded: Apple's Writing example ("Choose a password with at least 8 characters.") and the WAI tutorial's messages ("Use the format MM/YYYY.") end with a period, and Apple asks an alert's complete sentence for its ending punctuation; Material asks to avoid periods on single sentences and to use them on multiple sentences. Windows' trusted pages say nothing on it. Today's examples ended every message and description with a period.

decisions.text: A warning follows the error's timing (forms-validation-timing): it shows when people leave a field they changed, or on submit, and clears as they type; since the value is accepted, it never blocks the submit. A success shows only for a check people cannot make themselves, such as an available user name or a verified code, when that check runs; a field whose value merely passes gets no success.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#105 step 7, point 2), B, among: A, a warning like an error and a success on every field that passes (the WAI tutorial's in-line example after submit marks each valid field); B; C, no success in a field; D, a warning on submit only. No trusted source gives a warning a timing: it follows the error because it is checked the same way. The WAI tutorial confirms an available user name as people type (binary messages); Apple confirms only significant tasks, since people only need to know when something is wrong; Understanding 4.1.3 counts the result of an action, a success, and a warning among status messages. Android, Windows and Material say nothing on either.

decisions.text: With severityIcon none, the message's own words say its severity, a guideline the component cannot enforce: the component writes no severity word and checks nothing, since it cannot know where a message comes from. A project that cannot write its own messages (from a backend it cannot change, weak, or already starting with "Error:") adapts them itself, starting them with the severity's word and its language's colon ("Error: …", "Warning: …", "Success: …", "Erreur : …" in French) when they do not say it. With an icon, the icon's name says the severity and the message does not start with the word.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-26 (#103 step 22b) among: A, the component writes the word, one translatable string per severity holding the word and its colon (forms-severity-word as decided); B, the icon's name plus a colon string; C, a table of colons per language in the component; D, no word, the message alone, with the fallback in the project's own text (D1, chosen) or behind an opt-in prop (D2). The team: it cannot be enforced, since depending on the project you cannot know where an error message comes from; projects whose backend messages are weak or already start with "Error: " adapt them.

decisions.text: The severity's word is the component's, never the author's: with severityIcon none, the component starts the message with the icon's name (severityIconLabel, translated with the form's language) and a colon as that language writes it ("Error: …", "Erreur : …"), in the message's color and weight; with an icon, after the control or in the message, no word is shown, since the icon's name says the severity. The author writes only the fix.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#105 step 11, point 2) among: A, the component writes it without an icon; D, as A with the word in the semibold weight (the WAI tutorial's strong); B, the author types it without an icon (every message then depends on the form's placement); C, always the word (said twice next to the icon, "Error, Error: …"). Today's warning and success examples typed it next to the icon.

decisions.text: By default, a form control shows an error when people leave it after changing it, and every control is checked when people submit the form; it never shows a new error while people type in it, and an error clears as they type, as soon as the value is right, a new one waiting until they leave the control again (late to show, early to clear). A choice is checked when people make it; a check people try values against may run as they type. This is the recommended experience, not an obligation: a use case that cannot follow it chooses another timing, and never marks a control as in error before people used it.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#105 step 7, point 1), as the recommended default in terms of experience, acknowledging that some use cases cannot follow it, among: A, on submit only (Windows Forms; a fixed field keeps its error until the next submit); B, on leaving then live, the web's own :user-invalid (an error comes back at the first keystroke when people edit a checked field); C, late to show, early to clear; D, as people type (an email is wrong until it is complete).

decisions.text: Every form control's message says the fix, for every severity: an error is the instruction that fixes it (the control's verb and the thing asked for, with the format or the limit when there is one), an empty required field reads like any other error ("Enter your full name.", not "This field is required"), a warning says what to check and a success what was confirmed. It addresses people as you, without blame, robotic words (invalid), interjections, please or we.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#105 step 11, point 1) among: A, say the fix; B, the problem, then the fix, in two sentences (twice as long, five of eight messages on two lines at the field's width); C, state the rule ("Full name is required."), which repeats what the form's marking already says.

decisions.text: A search field that stands alone, the only field of its search form (a header or sidebar search), needs no submit button: Enter runs the search on every platform. On the web, a form whose only field blocks implicit submission submits on Enter without a button; Windows submits the query on Enter; iOS begins the search on the keyboard's Search button. The Search field labels its own return key for search (its decision search-own-key), so the form sets no label for it. Every other submitted form keeps the submit button of forms-keyboard.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#103 step 19, point 3) among: A, the Search field follows the other fields (the form sets its label, a submit button), only its Escape line corrected; B, the Search field labels its own return key and needs no button when it stands alone; C, as B but every search form keeps a search button.

decisions.text: Keyboard in a form, on every platform: the fields take focus in their reading order (WCAG 2.4.3); a form that is submitted has a submit button, and Enter (Return) in a single-line field submits it, while a multi-line field takes Enter as a new line; the form sets the return key's label for each single-line field's place, through the platform's own setting. On the web, where Enter submits from every single-line field (implicit submission) and enterkeyhint changes only the label, the label names the form's action (go, send, search, done) and never next. On iOS and Android, next on every field but the last, whose return key names the form's action and submits; Android's Next IME action moves focus by default, iOS moves it in the field's submit action with a focus state. Desktop keyboards have no on-screen return key. Android Developers' Compose focus and keyboard guides (develop/ui/compose/touch-input/) and text input guides (develop/ui/compose/text/), and Windows' input guidance (windows/apps/develop/input/), join the trusted sources.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#103 step 19, point 2b) among: A, nothing in the Forms foundation; B, focus order, a submit button and the return key's label per platform; C, as B but next on the way on the web too, with script moving focus on Enter instead of submitting; D, B without the label rule. The fields say what Enter does by their kind and leave the label to the form (enter-by-field-kind, #103 step 19, point 2).

decisions.text: On Windows, the required asterisk stays in the control's accessible name: the UI Automation Name is the label as shown ("Full name*"), never a version without the asterisk, and the control also sets AutomationProperties.IsRequiredForForm. Windows follows Microsoft's guidance there, which asks that the Name be the label on screen, rather than the rule that hides a visible mark wherever a required state exists (forms-required-mark-exposure, forms-required-voiceover), which keeps holding for the words on the web and macOS.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#103 step 16, point 3b) among: A, hide the asterisk from Narrator (AutomationProperties.Name without it), IsRequiredForForm alone saying required, as the web and macOS hide "(required)"; B, keep it in the Name, as Android does (chosen, recommended). The team asked to follow the Windows recommendation for Windows specificities. The UI Automation reference says the Name should be the same as the label text on screen and not a modified version of it, and Windows' accessibility guidance says the accessible name of a form element should be its displayed label; neither page says that Narrator announces IsRequiredForForm, which is only defined as a UI Automation property, so A could leave required unsaid, while B at worst says it twice (the asterisk, then the property). The two Microsoft pages were added to the trusted Windows sources for this decision.

decisions.text: On Android and Windows, the required asterisk is red: the error text color, global.text.on-base.functional.error.default, the color of the error message and of the error icon (global.icon.on-base.functional.error.default has the same value), at the label's size and weight, 4 px after the label (2 px in small), with no word space; the asterisk of the note that explains it is the same red; a disabled control draws it in the disabled text color, as its label. The words of the generic rule keep forms-mark-style. 5.79 to 6.12:1 in light mode, 5.30 to 7.06:1 in dark mode on levels 0 to 3 (text, 4.5:1).
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#103 step 16, point 3) among: A, the mark's own look (forms-mark-style: regular, the description's color, after a word space; recommended); B, the label's style (neutral primary, medium); C, the Figma prototype's red asterisk (chosen). The team chose C because a reddish asterisk is the most common rendering of a required field in interfaces, and asked that its red be exactly the color of the error message and of the severity icon. Material asks that the asterisk take the color of the text that explains it ("If required text has a particular color, use the same color for the asterisk"), hence the note's asterisk in the same red; Windows says nothing of its color. Noted on the sheet: red is also the color of an error, so a required field shares its mark's color with the error message next to it; the word or the asterisk, not the color, says what it means (WCAG 1.4.1). The asterisk gets its own tokens, since component tokens are never forked per platform and the words keep their look.

decisions.text: The required mark ("(optional)" or "(required)") sits in the label's (or the legend's) text after a word space, at the label's size, in the regular weight and the description's color (global.text.on-base.neutral.secondary), so the name stays the strongest text and the mark reads as a qualifier; a disabled control draws it in the disabled text color (global.text.state.disabled.default), as its label. The word, not its color or weight, says what it means. Measured on levels 0 to 3 and the sunken level: 12.09 to 12.78:1 in light mode, 6.65 to 9.28:1 in dark mode (text, 4.5:1).
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#103 step 16, point 2) among: Figma's red asterisk (reference only, rejected by forms-required-marking; red is the form's error color); A, the label's own style (neutral primary, medium); B, the label's size, regular weight, the description's color (chosen, recommended); C, the label's size and color, regular weight; D, the description's style (12 / 12 / 14 px, regular, neutral secondary). The team hesitated between B and D and chose B: when the mark is smaller than the label, the eye goes to it before the label itself, since it is the only element of a different size. A weighs the mark as much as the name; C sets it apart by the weight only (500 against 400), subtle at 14 px. Two cues set B's mark apart, neither needed to understand it, since the word says it (WCAG 1.4.1). The word space keeps the label and its mark one phrase in the accessible name; it measures 3.5 px at 14 px and 4.0 px at 16 px, near the prototype's 4 px, so no gap token.

decisions.text: Which fields a form marks is a rule of the form, not of each field: every form control that can be marked required carries the same property, markedFields (optional, required, none), and a form sets it once, to the same value, for all its controls. Each control draws its mark from its own required: "(optional)" when it is not required and the form marks optional fields, "(required)" when it is required and the form marks required fields, nothing with none, so a mark never contradicts the required state. optional is the default, the rule's default (forms-required-marking): a form that sets nothing follows it, and only the note before the first field is left to its author. none is for a control outside a form (a filter, a setting applied at once); the Search field, which usually stands alone, defaults to none.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#103 step 16, point 1) among: A, a form setting, optional by default (chosen, recommended); B, the same setting, none by default; C, a mark chosen per field (none, optional, required), with nothing tying it to required; D, no property, the author writing "(optional)" or "(required)" into the label. A is the only option where a form that sets nothing still follows the rule, and where a required field can never say "(optional)"; it is the pattern the team chose for the severity icon (forms-severity-icon-placement): one property with the same name and values on every control, set by the form, rather than a form component the system does not have. B makes the rule opt-in: a form that forgets it marks no field, against WCAG 3.3.2 and H90, which ask that required input be identified. C lets two marks of one form disagree. D cannot apply forms-required-mark-exposure (on the web "(required)" in the label is read with the name, then "required" again) nor forms-required-marking-platforms (Android and Windows cannot swap the words for their asterisk). The cost of A: a control outside a form shows "(optional)" until its author sets none; measured on the docs examples of the Text field family, 21 of the 25 Text field, Number field and Textarea examples are not required and gain "(optional)", the 5 Search field examples nothing.

decisions.text: A control with a warning keeps the accent warning border, which the Color foundation sets to the warning text's step in light mode, warning 600 (decision border-accent-warning-600): border, outline, icon and message read one color for every severity, and every severity's border passes 3:1 against its fill and the surface levels. The warning and success rendering is complete; its pairs are requirements.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#103 step 13, point 4, the closing WCAG check of the warning and success rendering) between: A, close as landed, the light warning border at warning 500 (2.95:1 on the subtle warning fill, the known issue of issue #119); B, the light warning border at its text step, warning 600 / 700 / 800 (chosen). After warning-on-base-600, the error and the success read one step for their border, text and icon in light mode (error 600, success 700) and the warning did not (border 500, text and icon 600). With B the warning maps the same way, and every pair passes: on the levels 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 / sunken 6.49 / 6.16 / 6.49 / 6.16 / 6.16:1 (was 3.27 / 3.10:1), 5.86:1 on the subtle warning fill (was 2.95:1), so the Alert's warning border and a form control's warning border pass against their fill too (WCAG 1.4.11); the accent warning Badge's border is 4.19:1 on its fill (was 2.11:1). Hover and active stay one step darker each. Dark mode is unchanged (warning 400 / 500 / 600).

decisions.text: The warning icon and the warning message read one color, as the error's and the success's do: the two roles keep their meaning (forms-severity-icon-color, forms-message-color), and the Color foundation maps the warning icon role to the warning text role, warning 600 (#765818) in light mode, warning 300 (#FFC61C) in dark mode (decision warning-on-base-600).
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#103 step 13, point 3) among: A, keep the two roles as the Figma library maps them (icon warning 500 #BD8107, text warning 800 #3E2D0C, 3.97:1 apart); B, the field's warning icon in the text color; C, the message in the icon color (3.09:1, under 4.5:1); D, the text at warning 600 with the icon at 500; F, the text at warning 600 with the icon in the same color (chosen, the team asking that it work like the error and success mappings); E, the field's message on the on-subtle text role. Warning 800 gave 12.36:1 at the lowest, two steps darker than text needs; warning 600 is the lightest step that passes 4.5:1 (warning 500 gives 3.10:1). In light mode, on the levels 0 / 1 / 2 / 3 / sunken: 6.49 / 6.16 / 6.49 / 6.16 / 6.16:1 for the text and the icon (WCAG 1.4.3 and 1.4.11; the icon was 3.27 to 3.09:1), 5.86:1 on the subtle warning fill. Dark mode is unchanged: warning 300 for both, 8.38:1 at the lowest.

decisions.text: The severity icon draws error for an error, warning for a warning and check_circle for a success, the Alert's intent icons, and is named after its severity ("Error", "Warning", "Success"). Its color follows forms-severity-icon-color: the on-base icon role of its severity.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#103 step 13, point 2) among: A, the Alert's glyphs, warning and check_circle (chosen); B, a plain check for the success; C, no success icon. A is the Figma prototype's and the Alert's: the system already says these meanings with these shapes, and the three severities differ by shape as well as color, while the message still says the severity in text (WCAG 1.4.1). B departs from the Alert and from Figma and reuses the Checkbox's glyph, thinner at 16 px; C draws icons on some fields and not others under one placement rule, and after the control a field would change width or keep an empty gap when it passes. Measured on the Text field (every size, both placements, light and dark, levels 0 to 3): the warning icon 3.09 to 3.27:1 in light mode and 8.38 to 11.17:1 in dark mode, the success icon 7.44 to 7.87:1 and 5.92 to 7.89:1 (WCAG 1.4.11 asks 3:1).

decisions.text: A control with a severity is filled with the subtle functional background of its severity, global.bg.subtle.functional.<severity>.default (error, warning, success), at rest and on hover alike, under its accent functional border. The value and the placeholder keep their colors. The Text field family is the reference rendering (#103 step 12, point 1, for the error; #103 step 13, point 1, for warning and success).
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-25 (#103 step 13, point 1) among: A, keep the page fill for warning and success, only the error tinted; B, the error's rule for every severity, the subtle fill at rest and on hover alike (chosen); C, the subtle fill with its hover step on hover for warning and success. B is the Figma prototype's fill and one rule for the three severities. On the fills, in light / dark mode: placeholder 5.50 / 6.55:1 (warning) and 5.55 / 6.48:1 (success), value 17.15 / 11.54:1 and 17.30 / 11.43:1 (WCAG 1.4.3); success border on its fill 7.17 / 6.16:1; the light warning border is 2.95:1 on its fill, the shortfall accepted in step 5b (issue #119), and keeps 3.09:1 against the surface (WCAG 1.4.11). C would make the severities differ on hover and bring the light warning border to 2.66:1 on the hover fill.

decisions.text: The message keeps the functional text color of its severity, global.text.on-base.functional.<severity>.default (error: #C01619 in light mode, #F88275 in dark mode), the same color as the severity icon. With the error fill, the error border and the icon, this completes the error rendering; warning and success follow the same roles (step 6, with #103 step 13).
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-20 (#103 step 12, point 3) among: A, keep the functional error text (chosen); B, the neutral primary text (18.01 / 8.47:1 at the lowest, the red left to the box and the icon); C, the neutral secondary text, the description's color. A is the Figma prototype's color and the icon's; the message stands apart from the description by its color as well as its size and weight, which matters most with no icon, where it starts with "Error:" so color is never the only cue (WCAG 1.4.1). It reaches 5.81:1 in light mode and 5.30:1 in dark mode at the lowest on the surface levels 0 to 3 (WCAG 1.4.3).

decisions.text: The severity icon reads global.icon.on-base.functional.<severity>.default, decided for the error (global.icon.on-base.functional.error.default), in both placements: the role of an icon on a surface, the same color as the message text.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-20 (#103 step 12, point 2c) between: A, the on-base error icon (chosen); B, the on-subtle error icon, the Figma prototype's #940E11, the role of an icon on the subtle error fill. In both placements the icon sits on the surface, beside the control or in the message, never on the fill, so the on-base role is the one whose meaning fits; it is what the Icon component draws for color error on a surface, and the icon and the message read in one color. Measured on the Text field (every size, both placements, light and dark, levels 0 to 3): A 5.81 to 6.12:1 in light mode, 5.30 to 7.06:1 in dark mode; B 8.41 to 8.86:1 and 6.96 to 9.27:1, in a red that differs from its message (1.44:1 light, 1.31:1 dark). Both pass the 3:1 of WCAG 1.4.11. Warning and success follow the same role (step 13).

decisions.text: After the control, the severity icon takes the size of the Button's icon at the same size (size.3, size.4, size.4: 20, 24, 24 px for small, medium, large), space.8 after the control, centred on it. In the message, it is 16 px (size.2), space.4 before the text, centred on the first line.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-20 (#103 step 12, point 2b) between: A, the Button's icon size (chosen; also the Figma prototype's 20 / 24 / 24 px); B, one Icon step per field size (16 / 20 / 24 px). A keeps the team's rule that a field lines up with the Button of its size, so a field and a Button carry the same icon; the box gives up 28 / 32 / 32 px. In the message, 16 px is the Icon's size next to 14 and 16 px body text, the message's size since the same review (Text field decision message-text-size). The icon is 5.81:1 (light) and 5.30:1 (dark) at the lowest on the surface (WCAG 1.4.11).

decisions.text: The severity icon goes after the control, at the start of the message, or nowhere, as one rule for the whole form: every form control that can show a severity carries severityIcon (after-control, message, none; message by default), set once per form to the same value. Choice controls (Checkbox, Checkbox group, Radio group) never draw it after the control: they offer message and none, and fall back to the message when the form says after-control. Text-entry and picker controls (Text field, Number field, Textarea, Search field, Select) offer all three.
decisions.rationale: Decided by the team on 2026-11-20 (#103 step 12, point 2) among: A, after the control only; B, at the start of the message only (recommended); C, both, chosen per field (chosen, with the team's precisions: no icon stays possible; the choice is made at the form level so that the fields of a form follow one rule; choice controls always put it in the message). Measured on the Text field family (all sizes, light and dark, levels 0 to 3): after the control the box loses 24 / 28 / 32 px (small / medium / large), so its right edge no longer lines up with a field without severity or a Button; in the message the box keeps its full width; the icon reaches 5.81:1 (light) and 5.30:1 (dark) on the surface in both places. One property with the same name and values on every control, set by the form, rather than a form component the system does not have: each control can render on its own (templates, Figma), and the foundation states the form-level rule. message by default, because it is the only placement every control offers and it keeps the control's width. No trusted source ranks one placement over the other; all ask that the error be said in text (WCAG 3.3.1, 1.4.1), which every placement keeps.

decisions.text: A control in error is filled with global.bg.subtle.functional.error.default, at rest and on hover alike, under its accent error border. The value and the placeholder keep their colors. The Text field family is the reference rendering (#103 step 12, point 1).
decisions.rationale: The solid fill validated in step 5. Its hover step (global.bg.subtle.functional.error.hover, #FCCDC6) brings the placeholder to 4.33:1 in light mode, under the 4.5:1 of WCAG 1.4.3; with the same fill on hover every pair passes in both modes on every surface level (placeholder 5.42 / 6.62:1, value 16.91 / 11.67:1, border on the fill 5.45 / 5.14:1). Losing the hover tint is cosmetic (1.05:1 from rest today), and the Figma prototype has no hover in error either. Rejected: A, the hover step on hover.

decisions.text: On macOS, a required control sets accessibilityRequired and a visible "(required)" is hidden from VoiceOver; on iOS, "(required)" stays in the accessibility label. "(optional)" is read on both.
decisions.rationale: Point 2's principle, each fact said once, applied to Apple's platforms. AppKit's isAccessibilityRequired() tells whether an element must have content for a form to be submitted, so on macOS the state says it, as the required attribute does on the web. UIKit's UIAccessibilityTraits and SwiftUI's AccessibilityTraits have no required trait, so on iOS the word is the only way VoiceOver can say it. Checked on the reference pages, no VoiceOver run.

decisions.text: Apple's developer documentation for its UI frameworks (UIKit, AppKit, SwiftUI) is a trusted source for Apple platform rules, beside the HIG and the Accessibility framework documentation.
decisions.rationale: The HIG says how a control looks and behaves, not what an element exposes to VoiceOver: whether a required state exists on iOS and macOS is only in the framework references (UIKit's accessibility traits, AppKit's NSAccessibility protocol). The team trusts Apple's developer documentation for Apple development rules. Only the three UI framework paths are added, the narrowest prefixes that hold these rules.

decisions.text: Each platform marks required fields its own way where it has guidance: Android with Material's asterisk, explained once and in the accessibility label; Windows with an asterisk on the label, explained once, and IsRequiredForForm, so the state is said by the platform. iOS and macOS, where Apple gives no mark, apply the generic words.
decisions.rationale: Options. A: the generic words on every platform, departing from Material and from Windows' Forms guidance. B: each platform's own mark where it has one, the generic rule elsewhere. The team chose B, the rule step 3 set for every platform-specific choice. Material asks for an asterisk explained once and included in the accessibility label; Windows asks to mark required input with an asterisk on the label and exposes the state with IsRequiredForForm; Apple's HIG gives no mark and asks to make clear that required data is needed before people continue (step 7). The asterisk departs from the generic rule on Android and Windows only. How "(required)" reaches VoiceOver on iOS and macOS stays open: the API references that would say whether a required state exists there (UIKit, AppKit) are not among the trusted sources yet.

decisions.text: On the web, "(required)" is hidden from assistive technology (aria-hidden) and the required attribute says the field is required, once; "(optional)" is read as part of the accessible name, since no attribute says a field is optional.
decisions.rationale: Options. A: "(required)" hidden, "(optional)" read. B: both read, so a required field says "required" twice (its name, then its state). C: both hidden, so optional is never said and can only be inferred from the missing "required" and the note, which is not read when tabbing between fields. The team chose A: each fact is said once. Understanding 2.5.3 lets "(required)" stay out of the accessible name when the required state is exposed another way, such as the HTML required attribute; MDN advises against announcing required twice; AccName 1.2 leaves aria-hidden nodes out of the name. The visible label still starts with the accessible name, so speech input by the label works. Names computed on the review sheet by AccName step 2A; no screen reader was run.

decisions.text: A form marks the fewer fields, in words, never with an asterisk. By default (more required fields than optional ones, or as many), required fields carry no mark, each optional field ends its label or legend with "(optional)", and a note before the first field says "All fields are required unless marked optional.". When most fields are optional, each required field ends its label or legend with "(required)" and no note is needed. The required attribute stays on every required control. Applied as is on the web; what assistive technology gets from the word and how the other platforms apply the rule are asked next.
decisions.rationale: Options. A: "(required)" in the label (WAI validation tutorial, H90 example 1). B: an asterisk after the label, explained once at the top of the form (H90 example 2, Material, Windows, the Figma library), red as in Figma or in the label's color. C: required by default, "(optional)" on the optional fields and a note at the top (WAI instructions tutorial: indicate required and optional input). D: keep today, nothing drawn. The team chose C by default and A when most fields are optional, so a form marks its minority in words and never needs a symbol explained: a sign-up form with only required fields gains one note instead of a mark on every field. Measured on the review sheet, light and dark, surface levels 0 to 3: the word in the label's color 18.02 to 18.98:1 light, 8.47 to 11.29:1 dark; the note 12.14 to 12.79:1 light, 6.65 to 8.86:1 dark. The Figma library's red asterisk (required boolean, on by default) becomes a departure.

decisions.text: Where the label sits is a layout choice; the anatomy fixes only the order and the association. The generic rule, applied as is on the web: above a field-like control by default, in a label column at the start when the form's layout asks for it (step 10), after the box of a checkbox, a radio or a switch, never inside the box (no floating label on the web). iOS, Android and desktop follow their platform's own requirements and constraints where there are some, and the generic rule otherwise; a floating label is allowed where it is the platform's standard way, as Material's text fields on Android.
decisions.rationale: Options. A: above by default, a label column allowed as a form layout, after the box for checkbox, radio and switch, no floating label. B: above only. C: A plus a floating label. The team chose A for the generic rules, as is on the web, and let the other platforms follow their own requirements, so Material's floating label is allowed where it is the standard. W3C places labels above or to the left of fields and after checkboxes and radios (WAI labels tutorial, G162, Understanding 2.5.3); Windows places them above and shows left labels as a Don't; Apple gives no placement rule; Material puts the label inside the container (56 dp) or adjacent to it. On the web a floating label needs a taller box: measured with Material's 56 px box, it stands 20 px above a 36 px Button, and a raised 12 px label and the value need at least 48 px, so they do not fit in 36. Above and in a label column, a field lines up with a Button of the same size (28, 36, 44 px), the label centred on the box. No token, CSS, template or theme change.

decisions.text: Every form control that can show a severity has a message part, after its description (after the options in a group). The Checkbox, which has the error severity and no message part, gets it with the complex controls (step 2b), when the validator's warning about a severity without a message part becomes an error.
decisions.rationale: Options. A: state the rule now and give the Checkbox its message part in step 2b. B: state the rule and add the Checkbox's message part now. C: keep the Checkbox without a message part, its error said by the form (a summary above the fields). C leaves the error not next to the box and not associated with it, against the error-in-text rule, and relies on a summary that is not decided (step 9). B and A render the same once 2b lands (measured on a medium Checkbox: +23 px for a one-line message, the message 5.82 to 6.13:1 in light and 5.31 to 7.07:1 in dark on levels 0 to 3); A keeps the Checkbox's changes with the other complex-control points of step 2b.
